speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill C-209, an Act to amend the Extradition Act (appeal).

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Shall the Hon. Member have leave to introduce the said Bill?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Bill that I am introducing, seconded by Bob Homer of Mississauga West, is in response to the blatant injustices which exist in Canada today which permit fugitives such as Charles Ng and Joseph Kindler entry into our country to seek haven from foreign authorities, with more legal avenues and opportunities than what is available to a Canadian citizen who is accused of committing a crime here in Canada. To add insult to injury, our Government is spending millions of dollars harbouring these fugitives as they endeavour to escape justice.
The purpose of this Bill, entitled an Act to amend the Extradition Act, will be to streamline the extradition process now in place in Canada by first eliminating the fugitives' right to apply for a writ of habeas corpus and substitute it with a straight appeal before the relevant provincial court of appeal, and second, by removing any appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. This Bill will limit the number of recourses a fugitive has available to only one level of appeal. This Bill will also provide the Minister of Justice with the option to release the fugitive into the hands of foreign authorities either immediately or wait until the fugitive has been dealt with fully by the
Canadian penal system; meaning that fugitives will not have to complete their sentence here in Canada before being extradited.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill, also seconded by the Member from Mississauga West (Mr. Horner) entitled an Act to amend the Criminal Code and the Supreme Court Act, will limit the recourses available to a fugitive in this country by amending both the Criminal Code and the Supreme Court Act to remove any possible right to appeal a habeas corpus judgment to either the Provincial Court of Appeal or the Supreme Court of Canada. This Bill will provide the appropriate amendments to ensure that there is only one appeal stage; i.e., the writ of habeas corpus available to a fugitive committed to prison under the Extradition Act before the case is handed over to the Minister of Justice. It is my hope that this Bill will tighten up the extradition process in this country, a process which is weighed down heavily by inadequacies, illustrated most recently by the cases of Charles Ng, Joseph Kindler and many others who have been able to prolong their stay in our country through the costly and timely use of our legal system.
In summary, it eliminates appeal to the Provincial Court of Appeal. It eliminates appeal to the Supreme Court. It leaves the fugitive with only the writ of habeas corpus.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. We had an unfortunate incident on Parliament Hill last Friday. The hostage-taking caused some positions to be taken and some reactions to it. Being one of the Members who were here and could see with my own eyes how the forces and House of Commons security reacted, I would like, on behalf of all Members of my party, for the Liberals in any case, and probably on behalf of all other Members too, to say that we were very impressed.

We were very impressed with the way the security staff handled themselves on Friday. I want them to know that we thank them and tell them that we appreciate very much the difficult situation they were in on Friday. We hope that they are each individually given our thanks by the Sergeant at Arms who did an excellent job also.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, rise on behalf of my caucus. We held a caucus meeting this morning, and indeed all the caucus members present wanted to reflect their appreciation for the excellent work done by our security people.
Over the weekend, we heard a great deal of positive reaction and accolades given to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Ottawa Police Force. Those of us who were in the building at the time could only be impressed with the way our security forces went about their work. The initiation of their emergency response plan was first-class. Let us hope that they never have to introduce that emergency response plan again.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in the Conservative Party feel almost the same way. It was a wonderful response.

I was in the Chamber on Friday and I believe that the situation was well handled. The staff of the Whip's office held a staff meeting this morning in which we reviewed the past week. That meeting was adjourned on Friday when we were asked to leave the House, so we carried on with it this morning. At that meeting I learned that the response of staff members throughout the Hill was very positive.
The Address-Mr. Pronovost
Members' staff and the staff that served the House so well all felt some comfort with the response that came from our security forces. They felt that people knew what they were doing and that it was handled expeditiously and well. I would like to congratulate the Sergeant at Arms and his people for that response and tell them that indeed, all members of this Hill community can take comfort from the response. When faced with a challenge, they rose to it.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As Hon. Members know, there will, of course, be a full review of the security procedures which we have in the House and we will try to do that as quickly and as expeditiously as possible.
I thank the Hon. Members very much for what they have just said. The reaction of all our security people was of the highest order and a relationship was established veiy quickly during the event between our own security forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, a relationship which seems to have worked effectively.
However, after an incident like this, it is, I think, appropriate to review everything that happened. As soon as that review is done by the Sergeant at Arms, it will be presented at the very earliest opportunity to the Board of Internal Economy. If at that time further steps, changes or additions are necessary, of course we will deal with it at that time.

I thank all Hon. Members very much for their statements, especially after an event that clearly was very dangerous.

I think we can all be very, very glad that events worked out as well as they did.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the honour to be speaking in the House last Friday when some unfortunate incident occurred-that event on Parliament Hill. I will tell you that it was quite impressive. And I would like to join the other Members who have already spoken about the professionalism of the police forces here on the Hill and of the House of Commons security staff.
Mr. Speaker, when we left on Friday, we were talking about a very important aspect of the Speech from the Throne: the priority which this Government has decided to give to the environment. I very briefly referred to the fact that as a Member for that constituency I had the opportunity on three occasions since the House reconvened to rise on the matter of the Saint-Maurice River pollution, while my predecessors, the two Liberal Members who sat here before me for 25 years, namely Messrs Chretien and Grondin, never found the way even once to rise in this House to condemn the Saint-Maurice River pollution and have corrections made.
I also stated this was quite understandable in the case of Mr. Chretien, as we realized last year when he rose to Consolidated Bathurst's Board of Directors. This is how Consolidated Bathurst thanked Jean Chretien for 25 years of silence, 25 years during which they polluted the Saint-Maurice River.
As witness to that pollution among others, Mr. Speaker, we had headlines last week. My constituents and other Canadians perhaps should be reminded that in addition to last week's PCB spill, earlier this year Consolidated Bathurst spilled 750,000 litres of sodium disulfite in the Saint-Maurice River at Shawinigan.
Consolidated Bathurst over the years injected into that river in Shawinigan 20,000 tons of pulp. Admittedly the company has undertaken a degree of clean-up. We reminded the president of Stone Container in Chicago it was essential that clean-up operations be carried out and this summer Consolidated Bathurst will begin removing a significant part of the matter that found its way into the Saint-Maurice River.
What was noticeable in the area last week was how much the whole issue of the environment was directly linked to the Throne Speech and my constituents' perception of this Government's responsibility. Also, the lack of professionalism of the part of the Opposition.
The Leader of the Opposition rose in this House to ask questions that should have been put to the Quebec's National Assembly rather than to the House of Commons. The Leader of the Opposition neglected to ask the one question that came under the Minister of Environment (Mr. Bouchard).
As far as Hon. Members to the extreme left are concerned, the NDP Socialists, they were the shame of New Democratic supporters in my area, Mr. Speaker. They are not listening to my comments, although they could profit from them.
Our socialist Members did not take a single opportunity to ask the Minister of the Environment some intelligent questions about the St. Maurice River and the Consolidated Bathurst spill. This so embarrassed the NDP spokesman in my riding that he felt obliged to hold a press conference to apologize for the Members of the NDP Caucus who did not have time to show an interest in Quebec.
We on the Government side realize that the NDP shows an interest in Quebecers once every four years, before election time, and we see the results today here in the House, Mr. Speaker.
Environmental issues will be a priority for Canadians in the years to come. I would like to talk about a specific case. The St. Maurice River in our part of the country is one of the most beautiful waterways in Canada and, if it happened to be located in Europe, would be one of their major, well-known rivers. The St. Maurice is well-known unfortunately, because of the pollution that has accumulated in this river, and today we can no longer enjoy its beauties as we have in the past. People cannot even move freely on the river because of the obsolete practice of floating logs that still continues on this waterway.
However, thanks to this Government's policies and the splendid co-operation that exists with the Government of Quebec, I am positive that someday we will be able to stop the floating of logs in my riding.
Mr. Speaker, there are also some very alarming statistics that should urge this House and, in fact, all Canadians to consider the matter.
In Quebec today, 30 metric tons of woodchips are left to rot on the premises of sawmills throughout the province. This is the equivalent of about 510,000 Quebec trees felled during the last few years. Every week, Mr. Speaker, another 6,000 tons of chips is dumped on the premises of Quebec's independent sawmills, the equivalent of about 100,000 trees a week which are simply wasted because pulp and paper companies don't want to use the chips that are already available. If we put a value
April 10, 1989

The Address-Mr. Pronovost
of $10 on every tree cut on public land in the Province of Quebec, pulp and paper companies are aiding and abetting a weekly loss of $1 million in addition to the $5,100,000 already accumulated at the sawmills. Meanwhile, pulp and paper companies like Consolidated Bathurst keep cutting trees despite the fact that all this stuff is just rotting away. It is time they started recycling.
It would be an effective solution that would not cost the Government a cent, but we must let the public know this is important for the environment.
I would also point out to the House that last week's toxic spill has prompted Environment Canada to schedule for this summer a toxicological and ecological study on the Saint-Maurice River with a view to assessing the impact of dioxin-, furan- and PCB-related pollution resulting from last week's incidents.
In that respect I want to commend the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard (Lac-Saint-Jean)) who did not hesitate a second to take a series of concrete measures in this case as he did when disaster struck along the Alaskan and Canadian coasts. Whatever Opposition Members may say, Mr. Speaker, we do have a Minister of the Environment who lives up to his responsibilities in all such matters.
In the Speech from the Throne the Government did state that the environment would be its second priority. Time has come for action rather than trying to look for scapegoats. Another Government objective is to refine the policy which is geared to the concept of sustainable development-interdependence between world envi-ronement conditions and economic growth requirements. With that in mind our Government has established the National Round Table on the Environment and the Economy which most quarters welcomed as a constructive step to undo the harm of 20 years of Liberal administration when environmental issues were never raised in this House in spite of the many urgings by the then Opposition to the Liberal Government.
My constituents are also deeply concerned about the deficit. In the mail I receive and in weekend conversations I have with the residents of the Saint-Maurice ridings people never fail to refer to the days when Jean Chretien was Minister of Finance and spent public funds as if money was going out of style. So today, unfortunately, as the Government we Conservatives have to re-assess the whole problem. We have to pick up the broken pieces. In the forthcoming budget the Government will make sure that Canadians eventually have again ready access to the kind of social services they deserve.
[DOT]	(1130)

Interest rates rise when the Government borrows too much. Everyone is aware of that except Members on the Opposition side. The more money the Government borrows, the higher the interest rate for everybody. As a result, it becomes more expensive to invest in new machines and to build new homes and factories. Money spent paying interest on the debt cannot be used for social programs. It is becoming harder to find money for new programs. Our social programs could suffer if we do not work now to lower the deficit. Since its election in September 1984, our Government has lowered the deficit in a slow but steady way. More needs to be done. The amount of money borrowed to pay for the deficit debt is still growing. As a result, interest costs are still rising too fast. Federal government borrowing is still putting too much pressure on interest rates. The deficit is falling because spending is being held down while the economy has been growing. Approximately 1.5 million people have found jobs. More businesses are making profits. Therefore, income from taxes has climbed at a faster rate than spending. The economy has been doing well in this country, and we must thank the Government for that. The Government's policy has been working.
[DOT]	(1140)
Lowering the deficit is an important part of that policy. Investment in new factories and equipment is at a record level.

Mr. Speaker, in my riding, over the 20 years that the Liberal Party was in power and Jean Chretien was our Member of Parliament, we lost 12,000 manufacturing jobs. What a shame for the riding of Saint-Maurice! Over those 20 years, we saw the population of the towns in my riding drop dramatically. When Mr. Chretien was Minister of Finance in this House, the unemployment rate in my riding was 22 per cent, Mr. Speaker. It was a tragedy for our riding, which has lost a third of its population over the last 30 years.
During one week in 1983, three big companies-Gulf Canada, CIL and Dupont of Canada-announced that they were closing their factories in Shawinigan, all in the same week. During that week, Jean Chretien was in this House and nothing was done by the Liberal Government of the time to correct the mistakes that had been made! No special plan to reorient local industry was developed. Over the past four years, this Government has corrected those mistakes and is now preparing to do even more. Although that Hon. Member who represented my riding for 20 years was more interested by issues other than his

The Address-Mr. Pronovost
constituents' future, our Government has undertaken to make the necessary changes. I shall give just one example. This year, Mr. Speaker, we will open the most modem textile dyeing mill in North America, because the people in our riding, unlike those in the Opposition, said when the time came that they would get ready to face free trade the right way-with action. As for investors, Perfecta Dyeing has invested $7 million in the most modem textile plant in North America, with some substantial assistance from this Government. Thanks to the Free Trade Agreement, we will be able to take on the American textile market much more vigorously.
Where I come from, that is what we did and what we will continue to do over the coming years, Mr. Speaker.
I would like to refer to other projects. Last week there was a lot of talk about Consolidated Bathurst and their environment control problems. Company management are not blameless but they do have a positive approach in that field and we will encourage them to pursue their efforts along those lines. Consolidated Bathurst will invest $225 million in their Grand-Mere mill and a sizeable amount in their Shawinigan mill.
Mr. Speaker, we will be keeping a close watch on all the company investments to ensure that these projects protect the environment, that eventually the residents of the riding of Saint-Maurice may enjoy their river as it used to be, and that the Saint-Maurice River region become a first-class tourist attraction. The people of my riding know that the action of this Government concerning environmental issues will pave the way for a second economic upsurge in my region, yet they cannot forget the depression they experienced under the Liberals' 20-year regime.
Mr. Speaker, imagine for a moment a riding like Saint-Maurice which 58,000 people call home and which saw 12,000 manufacturing jobs vanish over the 20 years Jean Chretien was in office. Few and far between are ridings in this country which lived through such a depression, yet now this same individual has begun to speak in various communities throughout the country- behind the back of the Leader of the Opposition-intent on keeping Canadians heavily indebted and arguing that deficits are not important.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if Liberal Members in this House do not see to it that Jean Chretien remain in the private sector, we on this side of the House will do it for them at the next election.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to point out for the benefit of this House how utterly dishonest the New Democratic Party were during the last election in my constituency. The defeated NPD candidate crisscrossed the constituency promising the erection of 22 senior citizen community centres, although this is under provincial and municipal jurisdiction. Gentlemen to my extreme left, this is the reason why your candidate is not sitting with you in this House today, and this is the reason why for the first time in 97 years my constituency elected a progressive conservative member.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for recognizing me this morning; I will have other opportunities over the coming weeks to return to this matter, because the House of Commons in my view is the natural forum for this kind of debate.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I listened with interest to the comments of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Pronovost). He injected a bit of politics into the House of Commons. We are all aghast at that, Mr. Speaker.
My hon. friend indicated a concern about the environment and the fact that his Government has taken some initiatives. He failed to mention that one of the major initiatives taken by the Government was to cut programs for conservation and the development of alternate energy. Over the years, those programs have been gutted. The Hon. Member failed to mention that. I simply raise it for his information.
The Hon. Member also referred to the debt of the country. Under the Conservative Government the debt has increased almost 100 per cent. When the Conservatives took office the debt was $170 billion. Today it is in excess of $320 billion. On top of that, the Government plans to go ahead and purchase a very expensive fleet of nuclear-powered submarines. The Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice failed to indicate whether he supported the massive funding for nuclear-powered Hunter attack submarines. Perhaps in his response he will take the opportunity to indicate his position.
April 10, 1989

The Hon. Member also mentioned plant closures. I believe that we will have to get used to that fact, Mr. Speaker, now that we have signed the trade deal.
Over the past number of years the Province of Quebec has dumped an awful lot of its raw municipal sewage, both from industrial sewage and domestic sewage, directly into our water systems. Literally, hundreds of communities have been flushing toilets directly into the St. Lawrence River. This has been happening not only in Quebec, but I refer to Quebec because of the Hon. Member's constituency.
One of the ways to deal with that situation would be to introduce a municipal infrastructure program where the federal Government would participate with provincial Governments, which would participate with the local Government in one-third, one-third, and one-third funding in order to allow the local municipality to develop the proper sewage treatment facilities and the proper sewage and water infrastructure.
It is interesting to note that every single city and every single province in Canada agrees to participate in this funding co-operative. The only hold-out is the federal Government. The New Democratic Party has stated that it is in favour of supporting that type of positive initiative, as has the Official Opposition. Only the Conservatives have said that they are not interested in participating.
Every city, every province, and two out of the three political Parties in Canada believe in cleaning up our environment through the use of municipal infrastructure funding from the federal Government in co-operation with provincial and local Governments. How does the Hon. Member feel about that initiative? Would he take steps to encourage the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to introduce that in the upcoming Budget on April 27?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his numerous questions. I would like to point out to the House however that if the Hon. Member's comments are any indication, clearly that New Democratic Member did not invent the calculator. Looking at what he said on the accumulated deficit in particular, I think everyone can see the deficit accumulated mainly when my predecessor Mr. Chretien and the Leader of the Opposition were ministers of Finance cannot disappear in a matter of months. I think that is quite clear.
The Address-Mr. Pronovost
This is why I would invite the Hon. New Democratic Member to take his calculator one more time and figure that out. Because if by any chance we could have made that deficit disappear within one year, immediately the Hon. Member would have risen in this House.
He always did anyway. He always rose every time this Government took important steps in a serious, competent, professional way to reduce the deficit over these last four years; that Hon. Member and his Party always advocated increasing the national deficit. It was never serious. Just like during the good old Creditiste days! And for that matter, I am reminded by many Western members of some Creditiste members who used to sit here and suggested we should print dollars with a dollar machine. In some way what some New Democratic Members are advocating is a modem version of the Social Credit we used to have in Quebec. Let us print dollars, Mr. Speaker, let us have a deficit! Not to worry, the debt will be paid back later on. Except that right now, nearly one-third of the national debt must be taken from taxes Canadian men and women are now paying, and we will no have no more leeway to pay it back further down the road because of the kind of mismanagement that has been going on for so many years, even though we would be glad if we could give social programs everything we would like to.
This is why this Government at this point in time, just as it has been these last four years, is committed to solve the mismanagement problems that arose during those previous years. Concerning the environment in this House, Mr. Speaker, as I said you only have to look at the kind of comments that were made last week. The Hon. Member for the New Democratic Party rises today to address the problems of pollution in Quebec, but last week, when we had a specific problem, no one in his caucus had a sensible question for the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Lucien Bouchard). No one in the NDP caucus, which shows an interest in Quebec every four years, bothered to rise in the House and address this particular issue.
Before the election, as I sat and watched the proceedings, the NDP Members all made a point of rising in the House and speaking French, and I congratulate those who did. But since November 21, Mr. Speaker, lo and behold, most Members of the New Democratic Party have forgotten their French, except perhaps for the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent).

April 10, 1989
The Address-Ms. Black
The NDP, which shows its concern for Quebec once every four years, has never been able to win a single seat in the province. And until the NDP learns its lesson. . .

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I realize that the Hon. Member is a new Member of the House. I wonder if he would not think twice about condemning Members of Parliament for not being proficient in the other language of our country? I want to say that many of our Members are working hard to become proficient in the French language. We are proud of that initiative, Mr. Speaker, and that effort. I do not think it adds to the House of Commons when one Member criticises another Member of Parliament for not speaking in one language or another.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the House that most Members understood what I meant. Before November 21 they did speak French, and now, after November 21, they don't speak French any more on the NDP side. Canadians listening to us today understood perfectly what I meant, even Canadians in NDP ridings.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for the NDP was upset when he realized, four months after the election, that his caucus no longer spoke French here in the House. Mr. Speaker, they are very upset.
However, the people in the Opposition may still be frustrated about the results of the election on November 21, but we are taking concrete steps every day to help Canadians clean up the environment in this country.
We have taken steps and we will take more, and Canadians don't need the Opposition's negative comments, an Opposition that today, especially in the ranks of the socialists, is unable to come forward with concrete alternatives when criticizing the Government's policies.
So far, Mr. Speaker, all the initiatives on environmental matters have been taken on this side of the House, and for that very reason I am proud to be part of this Government.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The period for questions and comments has now expired. The Hon. Member for New-Westminster-Burnaby (Ms. Black).

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to rise today to address this House in response to the Throne Speech given by the Governor General last week. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) showed his contempt for the Constitution of Canada by saying that he did not think it was worth the paper it was written on. Well, I would like to say that his comment would apply better to the Throne Speech and the comments that were not made on the issue of equality of women.
I have received many letters, Mr. Speaker, from groups and individuals concerning the Government's funding of anti-equality groups. How should they view the assurance of a commitment to equality in the Throne Speech in light of funding to a group which opposes women's inclusion in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms?
A recent article in Saturday Night quoted some Tory Members of Parliament on the subject of women's rights. I do not know if these Members actually said these things, but if they did, it does show an appalling lack of appreciation for what the women who have gone before us have done and for what was accomplished by the women who are struggling.
I speak of women like Agnes MacPhail, who was the first woman Member of Parliament and a member of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation who overcame incredible barriers to sit in this Chamber. I speak of the women of Canada who struggled long and hard to win the right to vote for the women of Canada, and I speak of the women today who staff shelters for battered women, the rape crisis centres, women who are still fighting and winning in the courts, women who are attempting to change policy and build a future where our children can live in peace with our world neighbours, each participating as full and equal citizens.
These women working together in groups to provide services and to promote positive change are the women who deserve support from the Government, not groups who are trying to turn back the clock.
April 10, 1989

Yet another example of the Government's failure to live up to its pretty words about equality is in the area of language training for immigrant women. During the election campaign, the Government threw some money at language training, but continued to refuse to remove the discrimination against immigrant women inherent in government language training programs. Government policy still makes it very difficult for many immigrant women to learn an official language of Canada and escape their job ghettos, as they are not eligible for the same training allowances as most immigrant men.
I was pleased to see in the Throne Speech, Mr. Speaker, that the Government is now prepared to bring its unemployment insurance program in line with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I hope that this means that natural fathers will now have the same parental leave benefits under the UI program as do adoptive fathers. I sincerely hope that it does not mean that all adoptive benefits will be taken away. This Government has deliberately imposed inequality on young Canadian families by putting the onus on natural mothers to take care of infants.
In the Throne Speech, the Government promised to amend the unemployment insurance program to supposedly improve the program's fairness. Everyone who has suffered from this Government's idea of fairness has taken this to mean, especially in light of deficit reduction, cuts to the UI program.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. MacDougall) said that those who need UI benefits would continue to receive them. There are already many who need UI benefits who are not currently receiving them.
I received a letter from a woman in British Columbia who was experiencing a very difficult pregnancy. Her work involved standing at a cash register all day, and this contributed to heavy bleeding. She qualified for UI medical benefits for a time while she was going through this experience, but when the time came for her to then collect on maternity benefits, she discovered that she was ineligible for benefits because of medical benefits. Is this the fairness the Government is talking about?
Max Yalden, the Chief Commissioner of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, stated last week that women and visible minorities in the Public Service fare worse than in the labour force at large. I am pleased to see that the Government is finally recognising its failure in this area. It mentioned the task force on barriers to the employment and promotion of women in the Public
The Address-Ms. Black
Service. The issue of workplace discrimination against women and minorities is already well documented. It has been studied to death.
Women have been telling the Government for the past decade how totally unfair the Government is as an employer. We have already seen Nicole Morgan's excellent report on women in the Public Service to attest to this fact. I have a prime example of the Government's commitment to women in the Public Service. There is not one word in the Throne Speech about enforcing the Government's own employment equity targets or legislation. As well, in the area of pay equity in federal jurisdiction, employers are not required to prepare pay equity plans. This leaves it up to the individual to research his or her own discriminatory situation and make a complaint on their own to the Human Rights Commission. There must be enforcement.
All of this means that the Government has no commitment to equality, except on paper. The idea that I would like to convey is that if the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulro-ney) has a commitment to equality, let us see him enforce his own legislation.
Mr. Yalden also speaks of major delays in the Public Service pay equity study. This study has not produced any results in four years. I quote the Human Rights Commission Report:
Administrative delay and bureaucratic infighting remain more the hallmark of the program thus far than any genuine move toward pay equity. Either Government means business on equal pay or it does not.
I suggest that it does not.
The Throne Speech did contain one sentence about the Government remaining committed to a national child care program. How can the Government remain committed to such a program when it was never committed to a truly national program with national standards in the first place?
The one sentence in the Throne Speech about child care seems to mean that the Government remains committed to an inadequate piece of legislation. Child care advocates unanimously denounced this legislation. The Prime Minister's commitment to child care was so great that he refused to wait just a few short hours before the Senate passed the Bill before calling the general election. His commitment was so great that he stated on national television that he did not need to consult with child advocacy groups. Now I am very much afraid that with the Government's fetish about deficit reduction, it will be the children of Canada who suffer from deficit reduction.

April 10, 1989
The Address-Ms. Black
I want to commend the Government on its annouce-ment of a royal commission on new reproductive technologies. As you may know, this is a New Democratic Party policy and, as such, New Democrats have been calling for a royal commission for many years. It only goes to show, as others have said, that New Democrats have a policy that is worth stealing.
A royal commission is necessary. It is very necessary in order to gather information on how new reproductive technologies will affect our family structures, to determine the legal status of surrogacy contracts and of children who now have two biological mothers.
We need to think about what regulations are necessary to prevent the commercialisation of women's reproductive capacities so that poor women are never in the future used as baby factories. We need a royal commission that is impartial.
I have some concerns about the royal commission, however. These new reproductive technologies have been developed and administered overwhelmingly by men. It is important that at least 50 per cent of this royal commission be made up of women and for all of its members to be aware of women's equality issues. The mandate should include specific consideration of women's reproductive health and women's rights. Since the New Democratic Party policy on a royal commission was used, I hope the Government will also use the caring philosophy behind that policy.
I also would like an assurance from the Government that this royal commission will be given a mandate to travel across the country and receive input from women's groups and women involved in the process, as well as the medical and legal experts from all regions of Canada.
The Government has side-stepped the issue of abortion again. The Throne Speech contains only a vague reference to abortion, but absolutely nothing about the prevention of unwanted pregnancy, which is surely the real key to reducing the number of abortions in Canada.
Within the past four years the Government has cut the funding to Planned Parenthood by $61,000. The Government is now talking about cuts to the Unemployment Insurance Program, which comprises maternity leave, and economically harsh measures to cut the deficit, which will make it even harder for young mothers to survive economically.
I share the concern of my hon. friends who have spoken to the Throne Speech on the question of the universality of programs. The Government has already short-changed mothers and poor families by deindexing family allowance. I hope no other step-by-step destruction of the Family Allowance Program is planned. The Throne Speech seems to be rather vague on this matter.
In my riding we have two food banks that have been running for a number of years. We also have children who go to school hungry. That is the reality of poverty. It strikes young children. It strikes senior citizens attempting to get by on very limited pensions. It strikes young families who are caught in a never ending struggle against a never ending cycle of poverty.
The spectre of homelessness is no longer unique to other parts of the world. It has arrived on our doorstep. It is our reality in Canada.
I am seriously worried that the Government has closed its eyes to the reality of Canadian life. I am worried that the attack on universality is an attempt to demean those who most need this economic security.
The Government has blatantly neglected the needs of many Canadians by failing to address the rapid acceleration of interest rates.
This lack of concern has meant that the worsening central interest rate policy is now at a critical stage. Arbitrarily designed to cool inflation in the hot southern Ontario economy, this policy is strangling development in every other region.
Why has the federal Government failed to listen to the Canadian Premiers who have called for moderation in interest rates? Why has the federal Government turned its back on the small business person in my home province of British Columbia, which, while wishing to expand or begin a business venture, cannot afford to borrow the money to do so?
Why has the Government turned away from the young family faced with skyrocketing mortgage rates for its first home because housing prices in Toronto are out of control?
If the Federal Government were truly interested in deficit control, it would realize that high interest rates contribute to the worsening of the deficit. It knows that its own Department of Finance figures state that a 1 per cent increase in interest rates per year adds $1.5 billion to the annual deficit. Instead, the Government seems to have chosen to strike out against those who most need the help.
April 10, 1989

It will slash the Unemployment Insurance Program at a time when cut-backs and lack of job development have meant that productive Canadians, who want to work, instead must rely on unemployment insurance or welfare benefits.
The Government will introduce what is perhaps the harshest, most regressive tax in recent history, a national sales tax, which will hit hardest at low and middle income Canadians, a tax which is nothing if not inflationary.
Women make up the majority of the poor in this country. Women make up a majority of the elderly. One out of every two unattached elderly women in Canada is living below the poverty line. The Government first tried to deindex their pensions and now in the Throne Speech has announced its intention to take away even more money from these poor women through regressive sales tax. Many low-income people do not file income tax returns. They will never see this sales tax money again, and they certainly will not see it in the form of social programs after government cut-backs.
The incidence of low income in my riding is 23 per cent. Almost one quarter of my constituents will be extremely hard hit by this Tory tax measure. Why does the Government not tax the 60,000 profitable corporations that do not pay any tax rather than taxing the families of Canada into poverty?
In a rather wonderous turn of cheek, the Government has suddenly seen the environmental imperative. Canadians may be excused for approaching this pronouncement with a tinge of cynicism, cynicism which would be unwarranted had we not seen massive eliminations within the federal environmental programs just a few short years ago, had we not known that this is a Government which has no national vision of the needs of Canadians. I would suspect that someone saw a poll which said that the environment was of concern to Canadians and suddenly the Government is talking about it.
As a Member of Parliament from British Columbia, I have several concerns over the present condition of future plans for the Fraser River. One third of my province is considered to be a part of the Fraser River
The Address-Mr. Robitaille
watershed. It has played an integral part in our province's economic and social development. It is one of the largest salmon streams on the West Coast and it remains a vastly important component of my constituency of New Westminster-Burnaby.
Such a critical system can no longer be taken for granted. The reality today is that the Fraser River is seriously polluted. Emissions from pulp and paper mills, effluent from upstream communities and erosion from decimated forests have endangered the Fraser River. It is time to develop a multi-faceted approach to this situation. We must work together to see that toxins are stopped at source. The need for reforestation is immediate. Closer monitoring and strong penalties must be enforced for those who continue to discharge pollutants. Now as at no other time in our history, it is the time for commitment to the environment. I join with other Canadians in saying that the Tory record is just not strong enough in this regard.
There is talk in the Throne Speech of a caring and a compassionate society. The Government is offering a spot of compassion to the homeless people rather than shelter and food. It is offering a few minutes of compassion to women rather than concrete measures to promote equality. It is offering compassion for the dead birds of the B.C. coast rather than any sort of effective action to prevent environmental disasters. In the future Canadians want a great deal more from this Government.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Questions or comments? Since there are no questions or comments, I recognize the Hon. Member for Terrebonne (Mr. Robitaille).

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to speak in this House as the elected representative of the riding of Terrebonne and on behalf of its citizens.
I would like to thank the people of my riding for having put their trust in me on November 21 last in a resounding way, with a majority of close to 23,000 votes.
Mr. Speaker, my intention is to be up to the task and that is why I am speaking today in this House.

April 10, 1989
The Address-Mr. Robitaille
The riding of Terrebonne is located on Montreal's North Shore. The Mille-Isles River from east to west and the Saint-Lawrence River runs along its eastern tip.
Cousisting mainly of the regional municipalities of L'Assomption and des Moulins, Terrebonne is the most densely populated riding in Quebec. With 92,000 voters and close to 125,000 people, it is the fourth largest in Canada.
Its inhabitants are mainly young people, young families, couples with one, two or three children, with both parents on the labour market taking an active part in the life of their family and their community. For these people, a promising future still means a lot.
Mr. Speaker, the future also means a lot for our parents, our senior citizens. Fond of our traditional values, having helped to build this great country, they are entitled to a secure retirement. They are entitled to it and they deserve it, Mr. Speaker. You will understand the anger they felt when they realized that that security may have been jeopardized by the irresponsible borrowing, the thoughtlessness and the total lack of vision of the former Liberal government which had deceived them. Let us make no mistake, Mr. Speaker, the national debt was not created by our government. We unfortunately inherited it in 1984 along with many other unpleasant surprises.
Although I recognize that recalling these facts will not help in any way to put things straight, it can be useful to do so if only to show these people that we are firmly committed not to repeat these errors, despite the futile criticisms of the Liberal and New Democratic opposition and their desperate efforts to bring back a system which nobody wants except maybe those who had the privilege to be associated with them.
My riding, as I have said earlier, is made up of two major regions where the extraordinary and "dynamic" development reflect this will to succeed and to excel, this openness and this determination to take up the many challenges awaiting us in the next century.
The people I represent, like other Canadians, are aware of the many problems facing us, but they are ready to tackle them. I too am aware of these problems, and like them I am confident that we have the capacity, the imagination and the intelligence to overcome them. Some might feel I am overly optimistic, but the truth is that I have confidence as a Canadian, our most precious natural resource, namely self-confidence.
What the people want, Mr. Speaker, is a responsible government, a government which gives them the facts instead of constantly trying to sweeten the pill for political or partisan considerations, a government which takes its responsibilities, which trusts Canadians and respects their maturity.
That is why Canadians elected us and why they did not elect you. The Canadian people want the truth, and the Throne Speech gives an accurate picture of the current situation in this country and a clear indication of the Government's intentions and its firm resolve to act responsibly where others have failed to do so.
Since 1984, Canada's economic performance has outpaced virtually all of the world's major industrialized nations. Revenues increased considerably, and the number of jobs rose steadily to a total of $1.3 million between 1984 and 1988. The annual deficit has declined by approximately $10 billion. Our challenge is to maintain that expansion in a world economic environment that is increasingly subject to inflationary pressures. Our worst problem is not the annual deficit but the enormous cumulative debt we have acquired over the last 20 years.
Despite the Government's efforts since 1984, the interest on our present debt costs Canadians 31 cents of every tax dollar. That is a lot! Where will it all end, Mr. Speaker, if we do not take appropriate action? Forty cents, fifty cents of every dollar? No, Mr. Speaker. The answer is simple: Either we start paying today or we suffer tomorrow and send the bill to our children. We will not leave them that kind of legacy. Never, Mr. Speaker!
Like most Canadians, we cannot afford to bury our heads in the sand. During the next four years we will have to deal with the need to reduce the deficit while taking new initiatives. However, our work in the economic sector goes beyond reducing the deficit. The current federal sales tax is inefficient, inequitable and obsolete, and is costing us jobs. The present system favours imports at the expense of our exports and will make Canada lose nearly $8 billion in economic spinoffs and economic activity in this country. Our two opposition parties are well aware of this. We will replace the present sales tax with a fairer sales tax that will ensure the Canadian economy is fully competitive and that will maintain a stable source of revenues to finance social programs.
However, Mr. Speaker, to me the most important measure in this Throne Speech is the decision to develop the skills of Canadians. It means we will adopt a comprehensive human resource strategy for the 1990s,
April 10, 1989

which will include literacy, education, training and re-training programs. Like the people in my riding, Canadians don't want to spend years on unemployment insurance. They don't want charity. They want to earn an honest living, with dignity. They want good jobs. They want to acquire the skills they need to get those jobs.
Our objective will be to make the Unemployment Insurance Program fairer and more effective by directing more resources toward active training, to help people find other jobs or simply better jobs, instead of paying them for doing nothing.
By maintaining our efforts to reduce the deficit and bring down inflation and interest rates, and especially to guarantee the continued existence of our social programs; through the reform of federal sales tax; with a sustained commitment to multilateral negotiations; through investment in new technology; by continuing our approach to regional development; by updating our trade legislation; through further privatization; and with a human resource strategy for the 1990s, we will be able to build a stronger and more competitive economy. To sum up, an economy that leads to the kind of jobs and prosperity needed to sustain our quality of life, the quality of life of every Canadian man and woman. This is what the people want. This is what we have been elected for, and this is what we are going to achieve, Mr. Speaker.
As I said earlier, the eastern part of my constituency borders on the great St. Lawrence River. Furthermore, two important rivers, the Mille Isles and the Assomption flow through my constituency. River pollution and environment problems are a daily fact of life in my constituency. I need not tell you, Mr. Speaker, that this is of real concern to my constituents. Just like them, I am very much aware of the actions and intentions put forward by this Government in the Throne Speech.
I must add that the steps taken over these last four years by this Government, as well as the $ 110-million clean-up plan for the St. Lawrence River, have met with very much satisfaction in my constituency.
The environment priority in the Throne Speech points to our concern for and commitment to the quality of the environment for every Canadian man and woman.
During the past year, the people understood that the world as a whole must face an environment challenge of unprecedented scale. We need not look for scape-goats, nor should we make this a near partisan issue. The time
The Address-Mr. Robitaille
has come for action. This Government's goal is to develop policies based on the concept of viable development, which meaning the interconnection between States, the global environment and the need for economic growth.
In that area, thanks to this Government's action, Canada on October 17, 1988 was complimented for its exemplary role in connection with the global environment. Dr. Noel Brown, from the United Nations Environment Protection Program, stated before the Association for the Control of Air Pollution, an international group composed of hundreds of members, that Canada set an example for nations around the world to follow in the area of environmental protection, and to quote Dr. Brown:
If a Nobel Prize were created for analyzing the complexities of
sustainable development, that is, making economic decisions that
respect the environment, Canada would be one of the candidates.
I believe that we should be proud of such comments that prove beyond any doubt that our actions and policies are sound and appropriate, and they encourage us to continue in the same direction.
With this in mind, the Government will participate in the establishment of a centre for the international promotion of sustainable development, to be located in Winnipeg.
Still along the same lines, it is important to mention as well that very recently, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) was given new responsibilities in order that environmental considerations would be fully integrated into the overall decision-making process.
Environmental protection depends not only on the Government, but on every one of us. That is why we will try to make all citizens more aware of environmental problems. An environmental partnership fund will be created and the manufacture and use of environmentally friendly products, as well as promotion and recycling programs, will be encouraged.
Mr. Speaker, let me now point out the remarkable work of two environmental organizations that started in my riding, namely the A court d'eau Movement and the Quebec Environment Foundation. Its founding president, Louis-Paul Allard, and one of its most active members, Arthur Dube, are doing outstanding work and making a most positive contribution to the environmental cause. We must work in partnership with these people who are devoting a large part of their life, Mr. Speaker, to their fellow citizens' welfare.

April 10, 1989
The Address-Mr. Robitaille
Environmental protection does not only involve reducing the harmful effects of pollution. It also creates economic opportunities.
We shall therefore encourage the growth of the Canadian environmental industry and research and development, not only to find solutions to our environmental problems, but also to find export markets for equipment, goods and know-how.
So continued government efforts for environmental protection, increased citizen participation and support for our environmental industry are the three key elements of a comprehensive environmental protection strategy.
Mr. Speaker, I know that I do not have much time left to conclude my speech. I would have a lot to say because the Speech from the Throne says a lot about it: there are many commitments in the Speech from the Throne.
Mr. Speaker, I conclude my remarks by saying quite simply to the House that the speech from the Throne fully meets the expectations of my constituents and of all Canadian men and women.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker... and of course we could talk about a number of other issues such as the ratification of the Meech Lake Agreement and the national day care program which is so important to the people of my riding. Unfortunately it was put on the back burner because of the uncompromising attitude of Liberal senators just before the elections. They did not feel like endorsing that project, and many others indeed. The Senate has to be the undemocratically elected House...
Mr. Speaker, the contents of the Throne from the Speech meet the expectations of my constituents. For all these reasons and to ensure prosperity for all Canadians, Mr. Speaker, I intend to support the motion concerning the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne moved by my colleague the Hon. Member for Calgary Southeast (Mr. Richardson) and seconded by the Hon. Member for Bourassa (Mrs. Gibeau).

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Questions and comments. The Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer (Mr. Rocheleau).

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened closely to some of the remarks of our colleague the Hon. Member for Terrebonne and, like him, I am very much concerned about Canada's current deficit. Still I would point out to
our Conservative colleague that his Government has been in office here in Ottawa since 1984 and that in that time the Canadian debt has doubled.
Mr. Speaker, I am also quite concerned over the fact that 30 cents of each dollar have to be set aside to service the debt. I appreciate that the Government has to find concrete solutions to reduce the Canadian debt and cut down the deficit, but it has to do so in such a way that inflation will not soar to the higher levels we had in the past.
Mr. Speaker, there is a question I should like to ask my colleague from Terrebonne. We have been told that the Government will implement a new sales tax to replace the existing provincial sales tax. I would ask my colleague whether discussions are being held with the various provinces about this new tax. As you would know, Mr. Speaker, several Canadian provinces do not have a sales tax, while the taxes levied by others vary widely from one jurisdiction to the next.
I wish to know whether the Federal Government intends to implement this new sales tax, what impact it will have on inflation on the one hand, and the current interest rates on the other. Knowing what influence interest rates have on Canada's debt, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that in the present circumstances and in view of all the Canadian provinces request to bring down the interest rates, the Government is moving in the right direction.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Hon. Member's comment and his question which I am pleased to address.
As to the deficit, Mr. Speaker, let me recall some simple figures. In 1980-81, you had a deficit of $13,522 billion which had increased to $38,324 billion by 1984-85. The national debt which was at $18,523 billion in 1970-71 under a previous Liberal Government had increased to $199 billion by 1984-85, to a projected $293,351 billion in 1987-88.
Mr. Speaker, it is clear that when we were elected in 1984, we inherited an annual deficit of some $38 billion. Even if we managed to reduce the deficit by $10 billion, it is clear that there still remains a deficit of $28 billion per year, and the Hon. Member will understand that a deficit is something that accumulates, and it did continue to accumulate even during the past four years.
April 10, 1989

The Address-Mr. Comuzzi
On the other hand, I could have understood if the Hon. Member had asked me the following question: How is it that our national debt was not higher over the past four years? It would have been higher if we had not taken appropriate measures.
Concerning the sales tax reform, the Hon. Member seems to ask whether we intend to carry out a sales tax reform. I think he is about the only one who is not yet aware of that. We have been talking about it for quite some time now and almost everybody knows it.
Even certain financial critics of the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party recognized before the election that our Federal sales tax scheme was somewhat archaic and inadequate.
As to whether there are negotiations, again I am surprised that the Hon. Member who once was a Member of the Quebec National Assembly is not aware that; yes, there are negotiations going on with the provinces.
The purpose of these negotiations. . . you will understand that I am just a Member of this House, I am not the Minister of Finance and I am not involved in these negotiations. Yet, I can tell the Hon. Member this: I trust that we will be able to co-operate with the provinces and develop a tax system which is more equitable and does not overburden the Canadian economy.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I listened with interest to the discussion of the Hon. Member regarding seniors and their entitlement to a good pension, to safety, and to security.
In speaking to seniors over the last few years I note that since 1985 there has been some apprehension regarding the Government and its attitude toward seniors and the security the Hon. Member spoke of that seniors are seeking. In particular, there are insecure feelings among seniors that the Government is not doing what it should to ensure that seniors can live with that security and that they have adequate pensions in order that they can live above the poverty level. There are inadequate pension provisions for those seniors who have not worked for a wage, but who have worked as homemakers.
Will the Hon. Member encourage his Government to work toward ensuring that the homemaking spouse is provided with a pension at least equal to that of the wage-earning spouse?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. Concerning our senior citizens, I should like to remind him, when he referred to their insecurity, that his Party and the Liberal Party did not hesitate during the last election campaign to alarm our senior citizens and foster insecurity. They are themselves the creators of insecurity!
Mr. Speaker, I should add simply that this sort of insecurity being felt by senior citizens is the result of the indifference, the deficit and the poor administration of a Liberal Government which over 20 years jeopardized our senior citizens' programs and security. I will urge my Government to take the necessary steps to counteract the dire effects of a deficit, a national debt which definitely endangers our social programs, namely those for senior citizens.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
On several occasions the Hon. Member for Terrebonne (Mr Robitaille) has stated that the Department of Finance was going to replace the present sales tax system with a fairer sales tax system. I know of no sales tax system that is fair. It has always been my understanding that a sales tax system is regressive. It affects those people who can least afford to pay. The aged are affected by a sales tax system, as are young families with children. Information comes to us that non-prescribed drugs and denture work will be affected by the new sales tax system. Therefore, it really is a regressive sales tax system.
Does the Hon. Member anticipate that this fairer sales tax system that he talks about will affect those very people whom we, as Members of Parliament, are supposed to be protecting? Second, I would like to question his arithmetic. He has some confusion with respect to what a debt is, and what the deficit is. It is my understanding that the deficit is that which we do not collect during the course of the year, and the accumulated deficits make up the debt of this country. It seems that he is blaming the former Government for the accumulated debt. He seems to forget that four years ago, when the present Government took office, the debt of this country was $150 billion and today it is $322 billion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I have to say that the Hon. Member's time has expired. If I have unanimous consent, I will give the Hon. Member a minute to answer the question. Do I have unanimous consent?

April 10, 1989
The Address-Mr. Harvard

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief. I thank the Hon. Member for his comments. When he refers to a sales tax reform, it is clear that the Hon. Member and his Party played the prophets of doom and gloom by prematurely announcing to the public that medicine and food would be taxed, when we have just indicated that the sales tax reform is being negotiated with the provinces. It is certainly premature, and I warn the Hon. Member not to make such insinuation without knowing exactly what the sales tax reform will be all about. The Hon. Member stated that a tax reform is always regressive. Just to hear him talk, it is easy to realize that he adhere to the notion helped by the Liberal Party whereby all tax schemes are regressive; That party has always perceived that in this way.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, let me emphasize that if the Hon. Member feels I am somewhat confused about the distinction between deficit and debt, there is no doubt that the Canadian people are just as confused.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I welcome this opportunity to take part in the Throne Speech debate and to have some of my views recorded.
We got to know this Government quite well in the past four years. We watch with some fascination and considerable distress as it pursues its right-wing agenda. We know its extreme faith in the market-driven system to the point that it can be all things to all people. We know that this Government wants to align the Canadian economy with the economic model in the United States. Certainly the recently implemented trade agreement is a reflection of that. Of course, this has been reflected in the Throne Speech of last week.
We were hoping for something a little better, but I suppose that is unrealistic. After all a leopard cannot change its spots. I am afraid that this country and its economy will drift further and further into the jungle of unfettered capitalism. It is going to be more dog eat dog, putting profits before people, thereby widening the gap between rich and poor.
In the next few minutes, I would like to touch on a number of themes including deficit reduction, the need for a caring and compassionate society and, of course, the concerns of the West, particularly my home province of Manitoba.
Let us talk first about the deficit. It is, after all, the talk of the town and of the country. The present Government has raised the profile of the deficit to unprecedented heights, and it used last week's Throne Speech for that particular purpose. No one likes deficits. It would be better if we could clear the accounts and have revenues meeting expenses. The voters tell us all the time, especially in the past few months, that they want the deficit addressed in a very serious way. We as responsible politicians should respond to that in a responsible way.
Deficit reduction will have to be done in an orderly fashion and with sensitivity, and certainly it cannot be carried out upon the backs of poor Canadians. After all, they are the last who should be waging this fight. While there is a need to bring the deficit down, we do have to question some of the Government's motives. I ask the question, Mr. Speaker, why this extraordinary and sudden preoccupation of the Government with the deficit right now?
This preoccupation by the Government regarding the deficit started the minute the polls closed on November 21. Why was there not this preoccupation about the deficit during the election campaign? After all, the deficit existed during the campaign. Why was there not this preoccupation and this talk of deficit before the election campaign?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The deficit was there. Did that stop the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) of this country from making promises totalling some $16 billion? No, it did not. Therefore we have to question the motives of the Government. The deficit was there when the Government decided to purchase nuclear submarines. Did that stop the Government? No, it did not. So why this sudden preoccupation with the deficit? Why not six months ago? Why not a year ago? Why not at any time during the period when this Government was pushing the national debt upward from a level of $170 billion to where it is now at about $322 billion? When the Government was spending the money at that time, was it concerned about the deficit? It does not seem so.
I ask the question, what is going on with the Government? Is this some kind of a set-up? Is it a trick on the part of the Government to cut social spending? Is it a trick on the part of the Government to somehow weaken the institution of the Government in this country, thereby weakening our ability to govern ourselves? It certainly would fit in very nicely with the free trade agenda, would it not? So, Mr. Speaker, we have to question the government's motives.
April 10, 1989

I also want to talk about the need for a caring and compassionate society. I want to address that matter because the Government reminds us of its devotion to a caring and compassionate society, but of course we all remember what this Government tried to do a few years back concerning the old age pension. It is almost certain, if you can take Government words at face value, that the unemployment insurance program will be the next target. After all, the Minister responsible for UIC has said that only those in need will get benefits, and that has a kind of ominous ring to it.
It would be rather ironic at this particular time to be targeting the unemployment insurance program. I say that because in recent weeks and months, particularly since this Government was re-elected, we have witnessed and experienced in this country an unprecedented spate of mergers, take-overs, acquisitions and that has produced lay-offs and plants closures in almost every province. I think this would be a very bad time to strip down the unemployment insurance program.
Let us look at this spate of mergers and take-overs and consider where is the caring and compassion in that process. Some of the lay-offs took place without any notice or consultation whatsoever. The suddenness of such a lay-off to a worker is frightening. Workers are at work and one day are faced with the pink slip, their jobs gone with a simple handshake. There is no reason given for the lay-off, except for the general explanation that it is good for the company, good for the industry and will strength the operation and efficiency of the company.
One must ask the larger question: What is in it for the community at large? What is in it for the country as a whole? Does this increased concentration of industry produce jobs? No. Does it produce better technology? There is certainly no guarantee of that. Does it result in greater competition? Not often. Does it bring retail prices down? No. In fact, it would probably allow prices to float upward.
When we look at the spate of mergers we must ask what is in them for ordinary Canadians who are trying hard every day to eke out a living and support their families. In Winnipeg a couple of months ago we were told that one of our beer plants would be closed. Some of us who live in that city might look to that kind of announcement with some favour if only knew that we
The Address-Mr. Harvard
were not sharing only the pain, since there is pain when jobs are lost. After the announcement, one of the companies involved said that as a result of the take-over the company was looking forward to dramatic increases in sales in the United States. That is good news because one assumes more sales means more profits. But where is the benefit for the Province of Manitoba in this case?
If more sales mean more profits, more production and more jobs, will we be included in the action? It is not likely. If anything, some Manitobans will probably have to go elsewhere in the country to seek the jobs that may be generated as a result of the increased sales in the U.S. market. We have already witnessed that in the Province of Manitoba. Workers who want to live in their beloved province have had to go elsewhere to find work. We have to be sceptical. Big business in Canada is restructuring the economy. Very often, those of us in the region feel that we are getting the short end of the stick. While this happens the Government not only seems to be quite indifferent to the process, but in fact approves of it.
The view of the Government seems to be: "Let the marketplace decide. The marketplace always knows best". That is not the Canadian way. If Canadians had always followed the dictates of the marketplace, going back to 1867, it is quite unlikely that we would have had the transcontinental railway or the Trans-Canada Highway. We certainly would not have had the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the National Film Board or even the Canadian Wheat Board.
I also want to talk about worker adjustment. That is an issue that needs to be addressed in the wake of the implementation of the trade agreement, and which must be considered in the context of a caring and compassionate society. During the election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised that victims of the trade agreement would be taken care of. He was showing a sensitivity to anyone who may lose their job as a result of the agreement. I think many Canadians believed the Prime Minister and, toward that end, the de Grandpre Commission was established. Many of us not only wanted to believe in that particular process, we thought it would be serious and looked forward to its recommendations. That was not to be. Only a few weeks ago we were told that the problem is too big and workers who would be laid off or were already laid off as a result of the trade agreement could not be identified. Tell that to the victims of the trade agreement. They know.

April 10, 1989
The Government's failure in this regard is hardly consistent with its talk about the need for a caring and compassionate society. Of course, a Government that is dedicated to caring and compassion certainly does not trample on the low and middle income earners of this country. But that is exactly what it will do with the implementation of a national sales tax. It is a regressive tax that will tax every Canadian, rich or poor, for goods and services they require. It will be inflationary. In fact, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) confirmed that the other day when he said it would be inflationary.
The tax will be an administrative nightmare. There will be all kinds of red tape and paperwork. It will be a horrendous burden on the shoulders of small businessmen in this country.
What will the Government tax? It will tax music lessons, for example. In fact, a woman in my riding says that this tax is a direct attack on families and their children. The Government will tax haircuts, movies, cab rides, visits to the dentist, repairs to homes, tax on sales of new homes, life and property insurance, fares on trains and buses. The list goes on and on. It will tax services by credit unions and banks, services by lawyers, electricians, plumbers and painters. There will even be an application of this tax on services provided by commercially operated homes for seniors and the infirm. It will be a bonanza for the tax man. As a result of this national sales tax, billions of dollars will flow out of the pockets of Canadians and into the coffers of the Government. So much for the caring and compassionate society described by the Government.
There is also the issue of Established Programs Financing. The Government has weakened its commitment in the area of EPF payments. There has been a drop of 2 per cent in the growth rate since 1986. This has a direct impact on the health care system in the country and on post-secondary education because 71 per cent of EPF payments go to the health care system in Canada and the remaining 29 per cent goes to post-secondary education.
