subsubtopic: TERMINATION OF DC-9 SERVICE IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to draw to the attention of the House the recent decision of Air Canada to terminate its DC-9 service in Cape Breton. This is another economic blow to the economy of Cape Breton. Not only has Air Canada reduced the quality of service to the people of Cape Breton but it has also reduced the staff at the Sydney Airport. I find it interesting that tickets for Air Canada's smaller planes which are replacing the DC-9s are at the same price if not higher than the DC-9 fares. How can Air Canada justify this and then turn around and at the same time displace 46 permanent employees?
It is very clear that the Government of Canada does not believe in equality of economic opportunity for all Canadians. We in Cape Breton need a first-class airline service, and this decision underlines the fact that the Government of Canada is not really committed to regional economic development in that it is leaving that function solely to the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. The Tories have been arguing for deregulation for quite some time. Now, we, the people of Cape Breton, see the real impact of deregulation and what it will mean for smaller communities across Canada; namely, cuts, cuts, and more cuts.

subtopic: GRASSLANDS NATIONAL PARK-OPENING OF VISITORS' CENTRE
GRASSLANDS NATIONAL PARK-OPENING OF VISITORS' CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday at Val Marie in southwestern Saskatchewan, sod was turned marking the start of the visitors' centre for the Grasslands National Park. The Grasslands is Canada's 29th national park and Saskatchewan's second. This 350 square mile area will preserve for all time the last remnants of native prairie in North America.
April 10, 1989

The park not only protects the many natural features of the Grasslands but also saves endangered wildlife and birds and unique cultural and archaelogical treasures. Several million dollars will be spent for acquisitions and development in the Grasslands over the next five years. Land will be acquired exclusively through voluntary sale, thereby respecting the private property rights of ranching families.
Canada's national parks system is the only one in the world with such a grassland reserve, a unique ecosystem in the natural heritage of Canada. I congratulate both Governments and especially all those individuals and groups who persevered in making the Grasslands National Park a reality.

Mr. Speaker, on Saturday I had the opportunity to be at Queen's Park in Toronto to welcome the March on Poverty walkers as they arrived from across Ontario. I am from British Columbia and we in British Columbia know all too well the growing problem of poverty with our large food banks and our school programs to feed hungry children.
I read with alarm the New Brunswick Minister's task force report outlining New Brunswick's growing problems of poverty and inadequate housing. However, I was shocked and dismayed to find that in Ontario, the most wealthy and affluent part of Canada, there is also a growing problem of poverty. People on low incomes are being driven further into poverty by the total lack of affordable housing.
I call upon the Government to take steps to bring in the needed child care program, to increase funding for affordable housing and to insist that the provinces provide adequate income security programs. Canada is not a third world country. There is no excuse for having 20 per cent of our children living in poverty. We in the New Democratic Party demand that this Government act and meet its responsibilities now.

maintopic: TRIBUTE TO INUIT LEADER MARK R. GORDON
TRIBUTE TO INUIT LEADER MARK R. GORDON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to pay tribute to Mark R. Gordon, a prominent
Inuit leader from northern Quebec who died in Montreal on Friday. Mark was 36 years old.
Mark helped negotiate the James Bay and northern Quebec land claims settlement during the 1970s. He also served as president of Makivik Corporation, the organization set up by northern Quebec Inuit to manage the claim settlement funds. He was an eloquent spokesman for Inuit in the aboriginal constitutional negotiations with first Ministers over the last number of years.
All Inuit are mourning the untimely and unfortunate death of this intelligent and articulate young man who worked so hard for the good of his people. The aboriginal people of Canada have lost an outstanding colleague. Canadians have lost a leader of national stature. All those who knew him, including Members of this House, will remember him for his dedication and commitment. We will remember his contribution to the Inuit across the circumpolar world and to all of Canada.

maintopic: WORLD CURLING CHAMPIONSHIPS WON BY CANADIAN
WORLD CURLING CHAMPIONSHIPS WON BY CANADIAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday in Milwaukee, Canada's women's team skipped by Heather Houston and our men's team skipped by Pat Ryan both won their respective World Curling Championships. I realize that the rules of this House prohibit me from using this occasion for congratulatory messages, but as a frustrated old curler who has been trying for 30 years to draw to the four foot, I must at least take this opportunity to join with all Canadians who share the pride of having these two fine teams return Canada to the position of world curling supremacy.

Mr. Speaker, last Thursday, April 6, at least 2,000 Canadians of Lebanese origin conducted a peaceful, orderly demonstration on Parliament Hill. They were protesting the destruction, violence and terror which has plagued the citizens of Lebanon for 15 years of war caused by the invasion of foreigners. Their plea was strong and clear for Canada to use all its diplomatic levers through the United Nations to achieve peace in Lebanon.

April 10, 1989
Last Friday, an unfortunate and regrettable incident took place on Parliament Hill. Charles Yakoub, a Canadian who was bom in Beirut, Lebanon, apparently became overly distraught over the plight of his parents who live in Lebanon. Since the recent bombardment of East Beirut, his parents have been living underground with no water and no electricity.
While the bus hijacking incident will have to be dealt with by the courts, I know all Hon. Members of the House will agree with me that this one isolated incident which ended, fortunately, without harm to anyone, will in no way diminish the respect we have for the outstanding contributions made to our Canadian society over many years by the thousands of Canadians of Lebanese origin.

maintopic: WORLD CURLING CHAMPIONSHIPS-TRIBUTE TO CANADIAN TEAMS
WORLD CURLING CHAMPIONSHIPS-TRIBUTE TO CANADIAN TEAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like my colleague, I am pleased to announce that yesterday, Canadian rinks swept both the men's and the women's world curling titles in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. I am sure that all Hon. Members want to join me in congratulating the victorious Thunder Bay team of skip Heather Houston, lead Tracy Kennedy, second Diane Adams, third Lorraine Lang and alternate Gloria Taylor who beat Trine Trulson's Norwegian rink. This team showed the chief umpires that they not only came to curl but they also came to win. This marks the fifth time in six years that our women's side has won the world championships.
Congratulations are also in order for Pat Ryan's Edmonton rink. It is events such as this which make us all prouder to be Canadians. It reminds us that rural and small-town Canada are part of the fabric which makes this country so great. Good stuff, Heather! Good stuff, Bill! Good stuff, Thunder Bay!

subtopic: INAUGURATION OF A SCHOOL IN WASWANIPI, ABITIBI
INAUGURATION OF A SCHOOL IN WASWANIPI, ABITIBI
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 30, the new Willie J. Happyjack School was officially
opened in Waswanipi, Abitibi. It has 20 classrooms from junior kindergarten to secondary V inclusive.
According to the Cree School Board, that school has approximately 340 students. It costs $5.2 millions, of which $3.8 millions or 75 percent are borne by the Federal Government and the remaining $1.4 million by the Government of Quebec.
I am pleased with this achievement because I have much at heart the education of young Crees.
Mr. Speaker, I offer my congratulations to the people of Waswanipi for their action and their determination and my thanks to the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs (M. Cadieux)!

subtopic: EFFECTS OF EXPANSION PROPOSAL BY TRANS MOUNTAIN PIPELINE COMPANY
EFFECTS OF EXPANSION PROPOSAL BY TRANS MOUNTAIN PIPELINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, residents of the North Burnaby area of my constituency are strongly opposed to the increased environmental dangers, including air and water pollution, arising from the August, 1988 National Energy Board approval of an expansion proposal by Trans Mountain Pipeline Co. This proposal will mean three new storage tanks on Burnaby Mountain and a major increase in tanker and barge traffic in the Burrard Inlet, up from 15 tankers last year to 48 tankers and barges after the expansion.
We have seen the recent devastation caused by the Alaska oil spill and the West Coast oil spill, and we do not want to take the chance of a major disaster when Westridge terminal becomes the busiest hazardous goods loading dock in the Port of Vancouver. I urge the federal Government to order immediately a full environmental impact assessment of this dangerous proposal and in the meantime to say no to any expansion by Trans Mountain Pipeline Co. We cannot afford to take the risk of yet another major oil spill, this time in the sheltered waters of Burrard Inlet. When will the federal Government show leadership on this important environmental issue? When will the federal Government stand up, not just for residents of North Burnaby, but for residents throughout the lower mainland of British Columbia?

April 10, 1989

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION URGED BY SOCIAL STUDIES CLASS AT R.I. BAKER SCHOOL IN COALDALE, ALBERTA

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION URGED BY SOCIAL STUDIES CLASS AT R.I. BAKER SCHOOL IN COALDALE, ALBERTA
speechtext:
The grade 8A Social Studies class at the R.I. Baker School in Coaldale, Alberta, with guidance from their teacher, Mr. Perry Mirkovich, have just completed a project designed to inform and combat the sinister effects of acid rain. The more they learned, the more alarmed they became. They informed others in their school and through the mass media informed others across Canada. As well, they changed several of their own personal habits. They chose February 15, 1989, as Acid Rain Prevention Day and invited all secondary students in Alberta to write to the federal Acting Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard).
Their plea is as follows:
On behalf of the youth of the world, we, the grade 8A Social Studies class of R. I. Baker School, ask you, our nation's leaders, to place as a top priority the conservation and wise use of our environment so that the children of the future may enjoy the rewards of a cleaner world.

maintopic: RESEARCH, DEVELOPMENT AND EDUCATION RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE NATIONAL CONSORTIUM OF SCIENTIFIC AND EDUCATIONAL SOCIETIES
RESEARCH, DEVELOPMENT AND EDUCATION RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE NATIONAL CONSORTIUM OF SCIENTIFIC AND EDUCATIONAL SOCIETIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the course of this week, Members will have an important opportunity to meet the national consortium of scientific and educational societies representing over 55,000 researchers and over 450,000 post-secondary students. These people will be on Parliament Hill for the purpose of speaking with Members. They are here to talk about Canada's crisis in research, development and education and its impact on our national well-being and economic strength.

Their message comes at the right moment. The National Advisory Board for Science and Technology and the deGrandpre Commission both urge the Federal Government to take concrete steps that will indicate it is well aware that research and development is of paramount importance.

I call upon Members to meet with representatives of the consortium this week. I urge the Government to double the base budgets of the three research-granting councils and index them at a rate of 1.5 times the annual growth rate of GNP; to convene a First Ministers' meeting to discuss the crisis in post-secondary education; to expand federal government research in such vital areas as agriculture, health, the environment and space; and to modernize and increase funding for student financial assistance.

maintopic: WORLD CURLING CHAMPIONSHIPS-TRIBUTE TO PAT RYAN OF THE EDMONTON TEAM
WORLD CURLING CHAMPIONSHIPS-TRIBUTE TO PAT RYAN OF THE EDMONTON TEAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to ask the rest of the Members to join me in congratulating a Kelowna resident, Pat Ryan, who with his Edmonton team yesterday won the World Curling Championship in Milwaukee. As many Canadians will know, Mr. Ryan defeated another Kelowna resident, Mr. Rick Folk, for the Canadian championship.
This truly enhances Kelowna's image as the curling capital of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today confident that I speak for millions of Canadians when I express alarm at the lack of seeming urgency on the part of the Government to address the problem that has been created in this country when we have no legislation in place to protect the pre-bom. Under the heading of "A Caring Nation' in the Throne Speech, some slightly vague reference was made to abortion. I urge the Government to get their priorities in order and show a new level of humaneness and show real care for the pre-born who are the most defenceless in our society.

An ongoing steelworkers' union-sponsored survey into cancer-related mortality among former Sysco steel coke oven workers in Cape Breton shows, based on 103 known deaths, a cancer morbidity rate of 53.3 per cent.

April 10, 1989
Oral Questions
Despite these alarming facts plus government knowledge of information contained in two related "internal" reports by Environment Canada which have been "restricted" from public access from 1974, the attitude of both senior Governments has, according to the union, been "anything but co-operative".
Despite the fact that these workers have died and the ovens are closed, there is still a problem to solve. These workers-both dead and alive-and their families need help in establishing claims. Their community needs help in cleaning up the mess of corporate and government neglect.
The Minister of Health should agree now to the two-year request for a meeting with the union. The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) should immediately release the 1974 reports. The Government should move quickly to initiate the comprehensive community environmental study which has been recommended.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES - NOTWITHSTANDING CLAUSE-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully last week to the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) speech in the Throne Speech debate. I have yet to hear the Prime Minister make a clear, unequivocal statement about the Quebec language legislation. Instead of criticizing Mr. Bourassa for limiting fundamental rights in Quebec, the Prime Minister claims it is the fault of former Prime Minister Trudeau. The Prime Minister says that the 1982 Constitution is not worth the paper it is written on because it contains the notwithstanding clause.
The Prime Minister must recognize that a majority of his Cabinet, including the Deputy Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Health and Welfare, all voted for the 1982 Constitution in this House of Commons. At that time, the present Prime Minister supported Mr. Trudeau's initiative.
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Will the Prime Minister now state categorically that he deplores the restriction of language rights in Quebec and does not approve Premier Bourassa's or any other Premier's use of the notwithstanding clause to by-pass the Charter of Rights and Freedoms?

subsubtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES - NOTWITHSTANDING CLAUSE-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES - NOTWITHSTANDING CLAUSE-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of errors of fact in regard to the prefatory remarks made by my right hon. friend. However, he is asking me a question that I have answered many times. I believe a Constitution should unite all Canadians, and this one regrettably failed that test. I believe that a Constitution has a fundamental responsibility to render unassailable our basic rights. This Constitution provided for an override clause. I said that because of this, the Constitution was gravely flawed. This is one of the reasons I have worked hard with other Members of the House to begin the process of improving it. My views on the notwithstanding clause and its use have been made very clear. I think my right hon. friend would agree that that clarity is on the record.
As Prime Minister and as a citizen, I accept and always have accepted the Constitution as the fundamental law of the land. However, there is an obligation on me to point out what I believe to be serious deficiencies in the Constitution and to try to correct them. The Constitution failed the test of unity. The Constitution should bring all Canadians together, and it did not. Because it should protect our fundamental rights and it did not, I thought it was not inappropriate for me to say that this was a gravely flawed Constitution.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has repeated again this afternoon what he said last week, namely that he is appalled by the existence of the notwithstanding clause, yet I remind him that in four and a half years as Prime Minister, he had the opportunity preceding the negotiations of Meech Lake, and he took no action to remove it. I have taken the trouble of drafting a resolution. Will he agree to a recorded vote of this House of Commons this afternoon or at an early opportunity denying Parliament the right to use the notwithstanding clause? In constitutional terms, will the Prime Minister agree to a resolution to the effect that the House of Commons will not use its powers under Section 33 of the Constitution?
April 10, 1989
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I will be happy to look carefully at any suggestions that come from my right hon. friend as to how the Constitution can be improved.
The Constitution of Canada, I suppose like all others, is a living document that is amended from time to time, as are others in other jurisdictions, for reasons of new situations that the citizens and the Members wish to correct and improve.
I will be happy to look very carefully at any views expressed by my right hon. friend.
Almost unanimously the House supported the Meech Lake Accord. The principal obligation on all of us, given the leadership by the Leader of the NDP, the Leader of the Liberal Party, and myself, is to be as persuasive as we can with regard to those provinces that have not yet ratified the Meech Lake Accord, and to indicate to them how important it is for the future of Canada that the document, already ratified by the House of Commons, receive approval in those two provinces.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to help the Prime Minister take another initiative because I take the Prime Minister at his word. I have a resolution here in front of me. Is the Prime Minister prepared to accept a resolution that the House of Commons undertakes immediately never to use the notwithstanding clause? And furthermore, is the Prime Minister prepared to let the House vote this afternoon or at an early opportunity to delete the notwithstanding clause from the Constitution itself?

Mr. Speaker, normally this kind of discussion takes place beforehand among the leaders of the various parties in the House. I already indicated to my right hon. friend that I would be pleased to look carefully at any proposal he might submit.
First and foremost, we have a process that involves another problem with the Constitution. My friend raises the problem of minority rights and the notwithstanding clause. There is another equally serious problem, the exclusion of Quebec from the Constitution. And I do
Oral Questions
think that the Hon. Member for Shefford is right. Indeed, under the circumstances, it may be even more serious.
Now, together we have built a procedure that would finally allow Quebec back into the Canadian Constitution. It is definitely the national priority, because I tell you without reservations that for me, the Canadian Constitution without Quebec in it is seriously flawed. That is why it would take. . . We need Quebec in the Constitution just as we need Ontario. For me, the Canadian Constitution without Ontario would also be seriously flawed. Quebec was excluded. We must do everything that can honourably be done now to bring Quebec back in and that is what the Meech Lake Accord does for all Canadians.

subsubtopic: BUS HIJACKING-REPORTED LACK OF COMMUNICATION BETWEEN POLICE FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General. The hijacking incident on Friday raises some very serious questions about national security and the ability of our policy forces to respond quickly, effectively, and co-operatively with respect to acts of terrorism.
Reports indicate that Ports Canada police and the Quebec Provincial Police failed to notify the RCMP in a timely fashion. The RCMP only found out about the incident two hours after it began when the hijacked bus rolled onto Parliament Hill.
Can the Solicitor General explain to the House this serious and terrible breakdown in communication? Can he explain why Ports Canada, that is within federal jurisdiction, did not notify the RCMP?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Solicitor General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
subsubtopic: BUS HIJACKING-REPORTED LACK OF COMMUNICATION BETWEEN POLICE FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to point out to the House-and I think everyone is aware of this-that criminal charges have already been laid before the court, after the events that took place on Friday, and of course, that public statements on the incident should be made with extreme caution. I would therefore urge all Members of the House to be very cautious in this respect.

April 10, 1989
Oral Questions
That being said, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be in order, especially since the House is meeting today for the first time since the incident, to offer on behalf of this House and on behalf of all Canadians our warmest congratulations to the RCMP which acted in a truly exceptional matter, considering the circumstances.

subsubtopic: BUS HIJACKING-REPORTED LACK OF COMMUNICATION BETWEEN POLICE FORCES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
subsubtopic: BUS HIJACKING-REPORTED LACK OF COMMUNICATION BETWEEN POLICE FORCES
speechtext: I think that with me, all Members will want to commend the competence and calm shown, as the Hon. Member pointed out, by the RCMP, by our security here in the House, and I would say also by Members and their staff who quickly responded to requests that they evacuate the building. This is an important factor. It is a situation that does not occur very often. Mr. Speaker, we were able to demonstrate that the RCMP and its entire team were able to react quickly and effectively, and I think all Canadians are glad they were able to do so.

subtopic: REPORTED FAILURE TO NOTIFY ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
REPORTED FAILURE TO NOTIFY ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no question that the RCMP and Ottawa Police ought to be commended for acting responsibly, effectively, and professionally in bringing the incident to a successful conclusion. However, that is not at issue.
What is at issue is how the incident was initially dealt with, and why it took more than two hours before the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the national police in Canada, became aware of this hijacking.
I fully realize that criminal charges have been laid and are pending, and my question is not directed toward the criminal charges, but with respect to how the government agencies reacted to this particular incident. I believe the people of Canada have a right to know.
Why is it that Ports Canada police and the Quebec Provincial Police failed to notify the Royal Canadian Mounted Police immediately? Why did it take two hours before the RCMP became aware of this incident? Does the Solicitor General not believe that national security and the safety of Parliament and of those who are here was compromised as a result of that terrible breakdown in communication?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Solicitor General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
subtopic: REPORTED FAILURE TO NOTIFY ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is
important to emphasize here in the House that the security of Canadians is a major responsibility that we do not take lightly. We, and the RCMP especially, demonstrated that we do take the public's security seriously, and I think we made this clear on Friday.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to get back, if I may, to a few other points raised by the Hon. Member's question. I would like to say that throughout this incident it was clear that there was a very high degree of co-operation among all parties involved, including the RCMP, security on the Hill and other services including the Canadian Security Intelligence Service. As for other parties that may have been involved before, that is an important point. I asked the RCMP Commissioner to discuss the matter with the Director of the Quebec Provincial Police, and this has already been done. I personally spoke to the Quebec Minister of Public Security this morning to discuss the matter, and I asked the RCMP Commissioner to make a complete review of the situation and the sequence of events, because I have every confidence in the close co-operation that we receive from the Quebec Provincial Police. This morning the Commissioner assured me that the relationship was excellent and that there was very close co-operation with the RCMP, and I am convinced this will continue. There is no question about that.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. McMaster University at Hamilton, Ontario, is home to a nuclear reactor which is vital to medical and educational research and which serves hundreds of scientists and engineers from around the world. It is the first and remains the largest of its kind in the Commonwealth.
However, this facility is in jeopardy because the Federal National Sciences and Engineering Research Council has denied McMaster a request for upgrading and has also cut the McMaster nuclear reactor core budget by $600,000. April 10, 1989
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister of State (Science and Technology)):
subtopic: NATIONAL SCIENCES AND ENGINEERING RESEARCH COUNCIL
subsubtopic: MCMASTER UNIVERSITY NUCLEAR REACTOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the decision not to fund the McMaster reactor was taken by NSERC as it went through all the priority items on its agenda. In its opinion, the McMaster reactor did not have nearly the same priority as many of the other items that were on the agenda.
In terms of funding science and technology, let me remind my hon. colleague that it was this Government that put $240 million into the Centres of Excellence Program, an extra $200 million into the Granting Councils over the next few years, and $80 million into the Canada Scholarship Program, as well as $500 million into technology. That indicates to me that we take science and technology pretty seriously.

Mr. Speaker, if the Government takes science and technology so seriously, then why is research and development headed this way instead of that way?
My question is directed to the Hon. Member who was the former President of the University of Guelph. The former President of the University of Guelph has told us that NSERC is doing this because it has decided to do this. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to take part in this Address debate. The task at end is not easy and the mandate some of us are assuming, I feel, is very significant. Each of us has a part to play, and whatever our political stripes, it is not only a right, but a duty. No one in this House is taking it lightly. A country like ours, so large and diversified from one region to the next, from one city to the next, from one province to the next must be managed not only with vision, but also with wisdom and courage. No matter what Party is in Government or what Parties are in the Opposition, the objectives are the same: make sure that our very beautiful and complex country continues to grow, thereby ensuring that every Canadian has his place in the sun, plant his tree, can cultivate his garden and enrich his heritage.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, as the popular saying goes, nothing is free, you must pay for what you get. And if someone decides to mortgage his health, his life or his property, the time comes when he must suffer the consequences. This is a universally accepted fact. Everybody agrees with it, even if some often behave as though they wanted to forget that simple reality.
As soon as it was elected in 1984, our Government turned the page on a great many dark years because of the distrust and misunderstanding which had poisoned Federal Provincial relations and threatened the very unity of our country. It made strong decisions and took the necessary actions to help our economy recover and create the job opportunities which are the motor of our prosperity. It gave Canada a new international direction and developed at home programs to ensure true social justice.
I indicated in a speech I made in December that on November 21, Canadians had chosen a new direction. They selected a number of representatives to sit in this House and asked us to plan for their future as well as our own.
Last week, the two Leaders of the Opposition Parties replied to the Speech from the Throne. They mentioned that Canada had changed. It has changed indeed. But this country of ours is not only changing, it is growing, maturing, thereby becoming more complex. Also, Mr. Speaker, the ways to deal with issues have changed. The means which had proved economical for decades and even for half centuries are no longer adequate in today's context.
We are nearing very quickly the end of this century. Not only will we have the opportunity to live through this event which occurs only once every 100 years, but we will enter at the same time a new millennium. Years come and go as they have since the adoption of our calendar and the years 1999 and 2000 will obviously be no different. However, the turn of a century always takes on a particular significance. It is traditionally a period when people ask themselves questions, sometimes even worry about what the future holds for them.
We feel a need to label everything and, in certain quarters, this is accompanied by a strong tendency towards reductionism.
The affluent society which came into being during the 50's has rightly or wrongly been called the post-industrial society. This judgment was quite narrow especially since it did not encompass the whole world. Everybody wanted to get more than his neighbour. Many tried to increase their wealth with any thought being given to the consequences. The so-called post-industrial society was the leisure society. This leisure society was to emerge in the 70's. Machines would do everything. Robots would be at our service. The first half of the century had witnessed great strides in mechanization. But during that period, one might say the seeds had been planted. The harvest started to emerge in the 50's. There seemed to be no limit. Science and reason were in. They cohabi-tated in a sort of way which made superior beings out those who worshipped them. Scientists thought only in terms of correlation and, if the correlation was weak, there was no link. It was to be rejected. Statistics and scientific rigour were to define the intellectuals, those to be in place.
April 10, 1989

However, it is also in this century that nazism, reared its ugly head leading to the massacre of German, Austrian, Hungarian, French and other Jews. Reason was law, and science also, supported by scientific rigour, of course.
While man was inventing and producing more and more tools, he did not see that those tools were shaping him. He had also learned to measure time and he thought he could control it. He did not realize that, in the end, it was time that controlled him. Besides, at the end of his life, man always admits to himself that he didn't have enough time to do what he had to do.
Our challenge of today and, probably, of the next century will be managing moderation. Our entry into the space age will show us all the advantages and disadvantages of excessiveness. Certainly, we cannot and must not stop progress, just like we cannot stop time.
However, for that very reason, we must realize the need to harness that excessiveness and to let it operate within an acceptable framework. Our life cannot be successful without standards.
Therefore, we must prepare our entry into the next century and millennium if we want to solve that excessiveness crisis and prevent further oil spills which would destroy us. That world of paradoxical reality and double constraint must be accepted. There are other possibilities. However, we have become modem while preserving our values.
Another challenge, Mr. Speaker, is to harmonize tradition with progress. As Touraine said, we are living a crisis of modernity, a time of paradox, a time of double constraint.
In the last election, the Canadian people have renewed their faith in Mr. Mulroney, probably because they were still quite satisfied with his performance. They already knew that new times were coming. They knew that because they can read the signs and hear the alarms. They knew that we had to open up. They accepted the free trade challenge. They know that the coming years will not be easy. They know that we must set the tone and show moderation.
In fact, a nation's maturity and self-sufficiency can be recognized by its capacity to produce and develop while accepting restrictions. Last November, Canadians clearly chose a Government which can not only conform to demanding standards but which also intends to set even bolder objectives. That is what the Speech from the Throne announces, Mr. Speaker. And I am honoured to be associated with the exciting mission that the Govem-
The Address-Mr. Hogue
ment and our leader, Mr. Mulroney, have given themselves.
I am honoured to take part in the development of the country along the lines of the new courses and policies set forth in the Speech from the Throne. The challenge for excellence protects us from excesses while preserving the aspirations of the people.
Mr. Speaker, the Government has stated a few basic objectives, including the enhancement of those values which make Canada the unique country it is. The economy may be the subject of discussions in all circles and some people may be inclined to believe that the science of economics leads the world, but we must come to realize that economics stem from culture and values.
We must come to realize that economics depend on the stability of those values because the relation between economics and culture and values is one of subordination. There cannot possibly be equality between both fields since culture must essentially precede economics. In a reduction context one is often tempted to think that economics prevail over culture.
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne is a national unity commitment which is aimed at promoting the values which make Canada a unique country in the world. Indeed Canada is now considered to be one of the most dynamic, pacific and promising countries of the world. A foreign diplomat once said that Canada is a pampered country which does not experience serious difficulties.
Such is our outstanding achievement after slightly more than a century of history, a fact which has to be acknowledged in a very special way. As a matter of fact, in 1992 we will celebrate the 125th anniversary of Canada and the 350th anniversary of the foundation of Montreal. As we are wont to do, we will emphasize Canada's cultural wealth.
Our sights will remain set on the challenge of our country's cultural life and our rich multicultural legacy. We will improve the distribution of Canadian cultural products. Concrete measures will be taken concerning citizenship, and the Government will establish the structures required to further promote harmony between races.
There is no question of reducing everything to a common denominator and attempting to make all Canadians look alike. It is much more a matter of building on individual differences in order to increase the effectiveness of synergia. The country will thus be able to avoid a situation where power becomes the be-all and the end-all.

April 10, 1989
The Address-Mr. Hogue
In that case, the phenomenon of unlimited growth occurs. It is a cancer.
Mr. Speaker, we must be proud of this Throne Speech because it is uplifting, courageous and challenging with a sense of responsibility towards the future. Another aspect of this Throne Speech also has our support, the part about a caring and generous society. For Canadians, tolerance and justice are paramount. Our society is concerned with the quality of life of its people. We have always honoured our obligation to come to the help of those in need here and abroad.
The Mulroney government shares these Canadian values. That is why the reduction of the deficit is so important. It will allow us to maintain quality social programs for future generations. And that is also why, despite our passing financial problems, we will continue helping families and senior citizens with greater emphasis for low incomes Canadians.
Income security is but one of the many challenges facing our society. We will also table legislation providing for the establishment of a national child care program.
The government will pursue its fight against family violence, child abuse and drug abuse and support research on AIDS and the diseases of the elderly.
The government will continue to support the efforts of the United Nations and its organizations and to participate in peace-keeping missions.
And that is why we will continue to strongly encourage further progress in international disarmament and to give our support to those who work for peace in the troubled regions of the world. Our caring and humane country is founded on justice and tolerance. Those are the values underlying our national and foreign policies which are cherished by Canadians.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, under the guidance of our leader, Mr. Mulroney, our government will be active in the field of science and technology establishing centers of excellence and programs based on strategic technologies.
However, our most important economic policy is without a doubt the development of our nation's work force. Our government will implement a comprehensive human resource strategy for the years to come, and that includes literacy, education, training and retraining programs.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance who, as a good father should, will bring us back to reality in introducing a budget which will remind us that our economic resources should not control our lives. The budget he is going to introduce in due course will protect us against the dangers of immoderation. He will challenge us to new levels of excellence. Finally, I just want to say how proud I am to represent the people from Outremont within this Progressive-Conservative government, led by a great captain, our leader, Mr. Mulroney.

Mr. Speaker, what concerned me about the Speech from the Throne was that one of the most serious threats to our youth, one of the most serious threats to law and order in Canada was given just a passing reference in the Speech from the Throne. I am referring to the drug abuse problem in Canada.
While it might be glamorous for the media and others to talk about drugs in amateur sport, the real drug problem is with the young people in Canada. It was much to my chagrin that I noted in the Speech from the Throne that there was only passing reference, after the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) called it an epidemic several years ago. The problem is getting worse.
In a few short years we will have the same problem as that which exists in the United States with respect to crack. We have been fortunate thus far but there is no reason why the problem that exists in the United States will not find its way here.
It is for that reason I believe it to be a national tragedy that ought to be dealt with in a forthright fashion immediately. We know the problems associated with drug abuse. There was a parliamentary committee that investigated that very problem just a few years ago. Yet the Government does not appear to be taking the problem seriously.
We know that a lot of violence is associated with drug abuse, especially with crack abuse. We know what the root problems are and we also know the problem appears, regrettably, to be concentrated in the black community.
Why has the Prime Minister and the Government chosen simply to give it passing reference in the Speech from the Throne? What does the Government specifically intend to do to address that problem during the course of this mandate? It is one thing to talk a big game about the problem of drug abuse in Canada, it is another thing to do something about it.
The Address-Mr. Hogue
Will the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) give the same care and attention to this problem, the problem of drug abuse, that he has given to the steroid abuse by a bunch of macho athletes who are bent on cheating in order to succeed? Does the Hon. Member not believe it more important in terms of Canada's priorities to hold a Royal Commission of inquiry into the drug problem, the real drug problem in Canada? Can he assure Canadians that the Conservative Government will make it a top priority and will spend the resources necessary to combat that very serious problem?

Mr. Speaker, such a broad question would certainly require someone with much more specialized knowledge than I have, but it makes a former university professor want to open up and approach this issue from different points of view and really spend an hour discussing it. But I am still glad to have allowed two questions of this kind and such an important one as the problem my friend opposite raises.
I am not in a special position to evaluate the quality of the Speech from the Throne. Anyway, I did assess it and I said that I supported it and was proud of it. I do not see the point in being specific about programs when the Government announces its overall policies. The Government opens these various chapters, so to speak, presents them and, during the session, they will be filled out page by page and discussed with those authorized to do so.
My friend opposite knows very well that a newcomer to politics is not to presume he is something else. I know the difference between the status of a backbencher and the roles various Members have, the roles of the various people in this House, and my role is not to legislate or state my personal positions for the time being, or state the Government's position on issues like drugs. However, there is no doubt that if drugs are singled out or dealt with specifically, nothing will be solved-they are part of an overall problem. And that is why in my answer, I dealt much more with what Touraine was talking about, of this crisis we are entering, this paradox, where to some extent, balance in society seems to be giving way to excess. The problem of sense versus power, of moderation versus excess and the questions we must all raise about these fundamental issues will no doubt lead us to deal specifically with this matter of drugs in due course.

The Address-Mr. Martin (LaSalle-Emard)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last election witnessed the emergence of a novel, unique phenomenon. For the first time in many years Canadians started to discuss our future as a country. The election now is behind us. However, our collective reflection on this country's future has but started. The current Throne Speech debate in my view is closely linked to that reflection.

Having avoided the issue throughout the long election campaign, the Government has at long last told us where it stands. At a time when thousands of Canadian workers need help adjusting to economic change, the Government stands for extensive discussions. At a time when the gap between the rich and the poor is widening every day, the Government stands aside. At a time when virtually every nation in the world is seeking new ways to create new wealth and economic opportunity, the Government stands pat.
On Monday last, instead of providing us with a prelude to a new decade, to a new century, we heard the last gasp of the old. Rarely has a political Party in office been given such an opportunity to demonstrate vision and rarely has a political Party failed so badly.
The problem is not just what the speech contained, it is what it did not contain: a belief in the capacity of the Canadian people, working through their Government, to meet the challenges ahead. Therein lies a fundamental difference between Liberals and Tories.
Clearly, this administration does not share our belief in the capacity of Government to evolve with society. It does not believe that Government can be an effective tool to help improve the lives of Canadians. That, unfortunately, is the essential message of the Speech from the Throne. That is why the Government signed a very one-sided trade deal, giving away the veiy tools that a modem state requires to develop its economy. That is why it is dismantling Crown corporations without giving any thought to the creation of new ones to meet new needs. That is why it stands by as high-tech company after high tech company representing the industrial future of Canada falls under foreign control. That is why our social programs have been put under the gun for four years.
This administration claims that its hands are tied by the deficit. That is garbage. Its objectives are not economic, they are ideological, an ideology that went out with the potato famine of the 1840s. The deficit is a problem and it is a very real one, but its solution does not lie in taking a broad axe to our social safety net. Canada has created a network of social programs of which we can be proud. We do not turn our backs on the sick. We do not walk away from the poor. Now, however, the Canadian commitment to social justice is coming under attack.

Our universities and our whole health care system are under attack, as are our senior citizens. And now, for the first time in our history, the generation of people under 30 is not assured a higher living standard than that enjoyed by their parents.
Deficit, reduction, yes! But not at any cost, and certainly not without reflection. Because as long as we limit ourselves to that budget exercize, we are not concerned with identifying new, more efficient ways to deliver existing services. The end result is that our cities more and more resemble those in the United States, and the drugs problem is getting worse.
Of course needs are changing. And our ability to adequately meet those needs certainly must change in turn. But it is no accident that Canada today is recognized as a caring, welcoming society.
It is because we always understood that we could improve our living standards by helping each other.
That is what Canadians implemented. That is their vision of the Government's positive role, and that is what is lacking in the Throne Speech.
The Tories claim to be a modem Government. I think they are frozen in the 1950s. Will you tell me why, in the very year the United States and Soviet Russia begin the most promising series of arms reduction initiatives since World War II, this Government signs an order for eight to twelve nuclear submarines at a estimated cost between $16 billion and $20 billion, nuclear submarines that are obsolete on the drawing board, nuclear submarines, the first of which will be delivered in the year 1998 and the last sometime after the year 2020, in a world that will be substantially different from the one in which we are now living?
April 10, 1989

I understand that a month and a half ago the Prime Minister of the country went over to Europe to receive an award for the environment. I doubt if that was the reason he went. I suspect he really went in order to repair the Maginot Line.
We as a political Party on this side of the House believe in the private sector, but we also believe in the positive role of government. That is why we disagree with the unspoken message of the Throne Speech. It asks not how can you make government more effective, but simply how can you make it smaller? Dismantling is seen as an end in itself. Redirection, modernization and the institution of government are not seen as tools of contemporary nation-building by the Tories.
For example, no one disputes that government programs can outlive their usefulness, but the mixed economy has not outlived its usefulness, nor will it, because Canadians will not limit their reach. We are not saying that we should dig in our heels to hold on to every last initiative spawned by former Governments. Far from it. What we are saying is that we should not deprive the Canadian people of the programs and institutions they require to meet the needs of the 1990s.
For instance, the Throne Speech did not once mention "housing", and yet lack of adequate shelter is one of the most pressing challenges this nation faces.

Despite the fact that over 100,000 Canadians are homeless, despite the fact that one of every three tenants has to spend more than 30 per cent of their income on rent, despite the fact that countless Canadian families are losing hope of ever owning a home, this Government did not feel that housing was worth a single comment. Shelter in a climate such as Canada's is not a privilege. It is a right. Furthermore, home or co-op ownership is not just a roof overhead. It is also an important source of income security and community stability. In a society without roots, it provides much needed cohesion. Home ownership is the most important investment decision that most people will ever make.

By making it impossible for some people to become homeowners, you deprive them of their main reason to be involved in economic activities. If you want to see what happens in major urban areas where people do not feel comfortable and are no longer concerned about
The Address-Mr. Martin (LaSalle-Emard)
their environment, see what's happening to our American friends.

Canadian cities, going the way of their American counterparts, could well be the price we will pay for letting home ownership get beyond the reach of the average Canadian. That is why it was so incredible that housing was missing so completely from the Throne Speech.
As far as shelter for the homeless, transition homes for the battered and the abused, decent rental accommodations for countless Canadians, this Government's lack of concern is simply beyond human comprehension.

speechtext:
Hear, hear!

So far, Mr. Speaker, we have emphasized some of the issues which the Government has ignored in this Speech from the Throne, but what about those it did address? Again, it is clear that the Government does not understand how to use its resources to develop a strong Canada. It prefers to remain idle while hoping that everything will turn out for the best. One has to wonder. For instance, the same Government which intends to use its Unemployment Insurance Funds to finance training programs has been for over four years merely slashing funds allocated to the training and re-training programs. Under these circumstances, who could trust such a Government?

This Government talks of adjustment assistance, and then the chairman of its own panel says that such assistance may well be countervailable under the trade deal. Then the Tories would have us take them seriously.
The Throne Speech speaks of the trade deal. It is enough to send shivers up your spine. In the first round, the Tories gave up most of Canada's bargaining chips before they sat down at the table to negotiate. They gave up on FIRA. They gave up on softwood lumber. They did not get a single concession in return. What they did was to take a dive in the first round. What will they do in the second?
I will tell you what they will do in the second. What we hear now is that the United States is gearing up to attack our subsidy programs. We hear the Government questioning the cost of regional development. They are beginning to hoist the white flag and the battle has yet to begin.

April 10, 1989
The Address-Mr. Martin (LaSalle-Emard)

Anything else in the Throne Speech? The environment. The Government is quite eloquent about it, but the time is no longer for fancy rhetoric, but for strong action, because we can no longer think in terms of compromise.

Who in this House will forget the scene of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) sitting there, having entrapped the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) in his lethargy, the two of them denying that one of the greatest ecological disasters of all time, the Valdez spill, posts no present or future danger to Canada? Their refusal to come to grips with the problem before them symbolizes the failure of this administration's concept of government. I believe this will become the symbol of the Government's chronic inability to come to grips with the problems of the 1990s.
[ Translation \
Curiously, Mr. Speaker, this Government which refuses to look toward the future is not learning from the past. Problems exist. However, there is something we should never forget: the strength of a nation lies in its ability to overcome its greatest weaknesses. Canada's strength comes from its vast geographic areas and low population density. If our railroads became one of the greatest achievements of the 19th Century, it is because our territory demanded it.
If our telecommunication industry is today a world leader, it is again because the Canadian people demand it. When a great country meets challenges, its population lives up to the challenge and that is the message the Throne Speech should have sent out.

Canada requires contemporary solutions to contemporary problems. We face economic decisions of breathtaking opportunity. We face new social demands of unparalleled magnitude.
In both cases we will meet the challenge ahead only if government does not give up its ability to lead. Some day the NDP may well learn that government is not always the solution. On the other hand, it is time for the Tories to learn that government is not always the problem. Tories believe that the answer is cutting back, while Liberals believe in moving ahead. Tories believe in restraint, and Liberals believe in adjustment. For the Tories, restraint means eliminating programs instead of
making them work better; restraint means allowing people to drift along instead of helping them to move ahead.
Let us be clear about one thing. Canada will not be able to move ahead. Canada will not be able to keep pace, much less take its place in the forefront of the nations of the world by restraining innovation, opportunity, and growth. Instead, we have to ensure our nation's ability to adjust. Canadians have to come to grips with the global market-place. We have to adjust to a changing workplace. We have to adjust to new environmental norms. Government has a crucial role to play in guiding that very process.
How does government play that role? It does so through policies that open the playing field to many who have been sidelined in the past, such as senior citizens, disabled Canadians, and single mothers. It does so by ensuring a role for the private sector to carve out niches to meet the demands of an ever-evolving society. It does so by setting the stage for entrepreneurship and innovation.
In conclusion, it does so by rising far above the sterile role prescribed for it in the Throne Speech of April 3, 1989.

April 10, 1989

I have seen studies that strongly indicate that a national infrastructure program would increase the over-all efficiency of the Canadian economy.
I wonder if the Hon. Member could respond to the points I have raised?

speechtext:
I thank the Hon. Member for his questions.
At the time of the appointment of the Minister of State for Housing (Mr. Redway), having listened to his criticisms and comments in the House of Commons, I, and many Canadians, felt that at last we had a Minister who was going to take an interest in his portfolio. I need only refer to the unfortunate comments of his predecessor, the now famous Minister of the homeless.
Unfortunately, it has now become manifest that that appointment was a way of silencing a veiy effective critic by bringing him within the circle. From the lack of any mention of housing within the Throne Speech, it is clear that the Government has effectively shut up a man who, on the Government's side of the House, might well have been the conscience for vast untold numbers of Canadians who are now devoid of shelter.
The problem is not only limited to the lack of reference within the Throne Speech. It is manifest in the lack of response to the countless groups that have come before the Government and asked for an increase in aid, asked for a roof over their heads, asked for warmth in the months of January and February, and who have been turned away with a casual wave: "We will have to see when the Budget comes down", and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) then casually stands up and states that there will be nothing for the homeless; there will be nothing for the young people in this country who want to buy new homes; there will be nothing to provide co-op ownership, which is a unique way of sharing in property for those who cannot buy their own homes. There will be nothing because the Government does not believe that people should be helped.
The infrastructure question is very well taken. Time and again it has been demonstrated that the multiplier effect of the work that would go into building sewers and bridges, and improving roads, would repay itself many times over in jobs and tax revenues. Yet the Government refuses even to consider its responsibility in that area.
The Address-Mr. Martin (LaSalle-Emard)
More important, without any social conscience in any way, shape, or form, the Government stated that it was going to be concerned with the environment. One of the most important polluters of rivers and bays are major municipalities that cannot afford decent water or sewage treatment. The Government states that it is concerned about the environment, but it denies funding to municipality after municipality to clean up the water that we drink and the air that we breathe.
Our cities are in the front line of virtually every social problem that we face: the environment, housing, the drug problem, and lack of skills. To deprive our cities of the moneys that they require is to deprive current and future generations of the intellectual and physical sustenance that they require. There is no greater example of the Government's lack of conscience and lack of understanding of the needs of nationhood than the fact that its members sit there, fat cats, refusing to help out those people who live in an increasingly urbanized society.
The answer I give to the Hon. Member is one of great discouragement. As a rookie Member of Parliament I have been sitting here and looking at Members without conscience across the aisle. I wish that I could say that they will live up to their responsibilities, but unfortunately their record does not enable me to do so.

Mr. Speaker, again I thank the Member for his question, and I especially admire his ability to stay within context.
As far as the first question is concerned, the one having to do with the flag registration, the fact is that as a result of the unfortunate drought in western Canada a substantial portion of the Great Lakes fleet is going to be laid up. As a result of that, there are going to be jobs lost arising out of a crop failure in western Canada and some ships have been flagged out, ships which undoubtedly will be coming back into the Lakes next year when indeed the crops in western Canada begin to grow once again.
But the Member raises a very important question, and that is why in this country do we not have a merchant marine? Why in this country can we not have a tax system that will give us the same benefits that the Norwegians have and other countries which desire to see their own flags flying? The answer, Mr. Speaker, is again a failure to understand the laws of international commerce and to understand nationhood.
So I feel very badly and I would hope that the industry which has put forth a plan for registry of ships would be listened to.
On the other hand, you see, this is it. Here is an industry that would like to create jobs for Canadians, and the hard-hearted Minister says: "To heck with creating jobs for Canadians. I have got my job. I am a Minister of the Government. I do not need to create jobs." Well, you may want to deprive Canadian sailors of jobs, but the Canadian sailors are going to have their day of reckoning.
As to the second question, the Member made a clear statement: why we should give jobs to bus drivers when we can give them to locomotive engineers? I do not understand that. I think we should be able to provide jobs to locomotive engineers and to conductors and at the same time provide jobs for bus drivers and truck drivers. I do not think any Member in this House should be discriminating against any Canadian industry as the Member did in his question. I get carried away in the face of such inequity, Mr. Speaker.
Let me just simply say that my personal position on this particular issue is that I would hope that Canadians will never be deprived of adequate transport in the regions. I would hope that we would never find a
situation in the Maritime Provinces, in northern Ontario, in northern Quebec or in western Canada where train service would simply disappear. It would not be reasonable. Nobody should ever discriminate against the regions of this country, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
I took a little trip back through memory lane and read some of these speeches from the Throne in the 1960s and 1970s, and it was interesting. I have here a reference involving the environment in 1969, and I am reading a quote here. Water was among most precious of our resources, that Speech from the Throne said, "and evidence of past failure to rehabilitate our water resources is there for all to see".
April 10, 1989

The Liberal Party has struggled mightily with resources and with the environment, and I guess the culmination, came forward not long ago, on March 8th in The Citizen when Greg Weston of recent biographical fame noted that the Liberal Party, which was millions of dollars in debt, spent half a million dollars decrying the terrible state of a particular lake. "I have never been so angry in my entire life", begins the letter signed by Liberal Party secretary, Marie-Andree Bastien. It turns out that after spending half a million dollars, Mr. Speaker, raising a lot of partisan comments, that the Liberal Party through their spokesperson had to admit, and this is a direct quote:
When faced with the fact that this was not a dead lake but a very healthy beaver dam in a very healthy national park, I said to my husband, oh, my God, it's a beaver dam. A senior Liberal estimates the mailing cost to the debt-ridden Party of more than half a million dollars.
So it can be said, and I realize I am being partisan here, but I cannot resist the jibe, that the Liberal Party in this case does not know the difference between a beaver dam and a dead lake. So this is not a very reassuring example of a contemporary awareness of the seriousness of environmental concerns.
Mr. Speaker, our Speech from the Throne in this particular case does bear testimony that we have honoured the commitments of the last four years. I think it is fair to say that even the most partisan of critics opposite would admit that in the past four years our country is considerably better off than it has been, that we have systematically reduced the budgetary deficit for the first time since the 1950s, that we have created over a million jobs, that more people can afford housing, more people are in better economic circumstances today than they were when our Government came into office in 1984.
Mr. Speaker, housing was never an easy problem. I remember 10 years ago, when I was Minister of Housing for a short time, we were faced with the infamous AHOP program. There were three AHOP programs as the Member from Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) will remember. On top of that we had in Ontario the Home Ownership Plan. What was the result of all this subsidizing and paying people to live in houses? People were walking away from their housing, tossing their keys in and saying it was not worth it.
Mr. Speaker, there are no simplistic solutions for housing. It means that people have got to be given employment and that constructive measures have got to be taken, and this our Government has been doing over the past four years. But why are we faced with such a financial problem today? Environment does not just
The Address-Mr. MacKay
refer to a physical environment. We have to look at our physical environment, but we also have to look at our social, political and financial environment. We have one-fifth of the world's fresh water. We have the longest coast lines. We are a neighbour of two superpowers. We look out on- three oceans and speak several languages, including our two founding languages, and yet with all these resources, Sir, and all this potential, we have not yet quite filled the great Liberal Prime Minister Wilfred Laurier's prediction that the 20th Century would indeed belong to us.
We have seen a country like Argentina, a distinguished representative of which was in the gallery today, which in the 1930s had a gross national product and resources of the same as ours-my friend tells me he was from Brazil. Well, the same comparison could be made about Brazil. Countries with great resources and great potential do not always realize them. Potential is a wonderful thing to have, but it can be a heavy burden if it is not realized. So when we congratulate ourselves and say what a wonderful country we are, how unique we are, how fortunate we are, how sensitive we are, perhaps it is time for us to step outside our national psyche and ask how does the rest of the world look at Canada. Just maybe they see us as a very fortunate, large, rich country that has not been managing itself too well during the past couple of decades.
I think all Canadians must come to grips with the realization that we have to do better and it is incumbent upon us to make a lot better use of the God-given resources we have in order to manage our country and our affairs in such a way that we can protect the very social fabric that we have often talked about as setting an example to the world. We cannot in all conscience go on spending a great deal more money than we take in and not realize that somewhere down the line it is inhibiting our sovereignty, hindering our options and eventually will menace those very social programs of which we are so proud.
In 1971, when I first was elected to Ottawa and this place, the country's debt was less than $20 billion. Two years later, the gentleman whom some people call the Lather of the Modern Canadian Deficit-I would not say that but some people indicate that it is the Leader of the Liberal Party when he was Minister of Finance-brought in an expansionary budget to attack inflation and high unemployment rates while the national deficit at that point reached about $24 billion. Since that time the finances of the country have steadily worsened at an alarming rate.

speechtext:
My friend knows, if he and I were in business and owed a million dollars and wanted to save the old family farm and the business, we would have to raise a lot of money every year. Let us assume the interest at that time was 10%. We would have to raise $100,000 every year in order to keep that $1 million from getting to the point where it might cause us to lose everything. This Government, being in that position, did its best, as he and I would do, to bring down the defict by raising more money and attacking the deficit. Unfortunately, despite our best efforts, the debt stock has continued to grow. That is the challenge that faces this Government, faces this country and faces all Members of Parliament.
We have to look at what our basic economic picture will produce if there are not some fundamental changes. I believe it is worthy to quote a very great Member of Parliament and our former national leader, Robert Stanfield, who added when he was speaking to this House on one occasion, that a Conservative must be concerned about the effects of economic growth, what it does to our environment, what kind of living conditions it creates, what is its effect on the countryside and what is its effect on our cities, whether all parts of the nation benefit or only some parts, and whether a greater feeling of justice, fairness and self-fulfillment results from this growth, thereby strengthening the social order and improving the quality of national life.
Mr. Stanfield further added that the Conservative tradition has been to interfere only where necessary, but to interfere where necessary in order to achieve social and national objectives. Perhaps this is an answer to my colleague from Montreal who raised a similar philosophic point on behalf of the Liberal Party.
It has been said more colloquially that the difference between a Liberal and a Conservative is that if a Conservative sees someone drowning in deep water, 30 feet off a dock, he will throw him 20 feet of rope and say: "Struggle over, grasp the rope and we will save you". If a Liberal is confronted with this pathetic situation, he will throw 40 feet of rope to the unfortunate person and when he grasps it the Liberal will let go, run away and find another good deed to do. There are different ways to look for solutions for people in trouble.
Loyal to our traditions, a Progressive Conservative Government has proposed in this particular Speech from the Throne several measures aimed at achieving social and national objectives. This is not a Christmas tree approach that we have taken. Some Governments in the past have done this, but ours is rather a thematic approach. We have made a commitment to building a stronger economy, to protecting our environment, working toward a caring and compassionate society, fostering the values that make Canada unique and, of course, a commitment to national unity. I am very proud to be part of a Government which, in the Conservative tradition, strives to ensure that all regions of the country benefit from a healthy economy.
I am particularly pleased about our Government's commitment to Atlantic Canada and the continuation of funding for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and ensuring that the Government's procurement policies become increasingly responsible to regional considerations. The Agency in particular for which I am responsible is playing an essential role in the renewal of the entrepreneurial spirit in Atlantic Canada. Through a direct assistance program, through an advocacy role, its co-operation and co-ordination mandates, ACOA has already levered more than $2 billion of private investments and assisted in the creation of over 10,000 new jobs.
As Minister responsible for this Agency, I want to assure the House and colleagues that I will do my best to ensure that ACOA remains responsive to the region's needs through extensive consultation with the business community, academe, labour and all other interested parties. Many believe that ACOA should be encouraged to play a bigger role in assisting entrepreneurs to find new markets, to obtain adequate business management training, benefit from export opportunities arising from the Free Trade Agreement and, in other words, to help this country move into the 21st century by adopting new technologies, new techniques with help for all those who require it in the small and medium business sector.
April 10, 1989

The consultation process yet to be announced will aim to determine whether ACOA's policy framework is adequate or if it should be adjusted, as my colleague has suggested, to meet present and future challenges facing Atlantic Canada's entrepreneurs.
In closing, I look forward to the implementation of the Government's objectives as set out in the Speech from the Throne. As an Atlantic Canadian, I believe that economic and social measures such as the reform of the Unemployment Insurance Program, more responsive procurement policies, the work of ACOA, and working toward a national child care program will ensure that our region benefits from a healthier economy, therefore ensuring a better quality of life for all Canadians. At the same time I cannot resist putting on the record in the House one of my favourite quotes from a great American who, as part of that select group of Americans who helped to build that great republic, had pretty definite ideas on the role of government. Thomas Jefferson said:
I place economy among the first and most important virtues, and public debt as the greatest of dangers to be feared. To preserve our independence, we must not let our rulers load us with perpetual debt. If we run into such debts, we must be taxed in our meat and drink, in our necessities and in our comforts, in our labour and in our amusements. There is some truth in that, although it was spoken a long time ago. While it is tempting for all of us to expect the Government to do a great deal to help, as well it should, there is also some truth in the maxim that any Government that is big enough to give you all you want is also big enough to take all you have got.

Connaught was Canadian owned. Lumonics was Canadian owned. One of the problems for research and development in this country is that Canadian companies are where we find research being done. The difficulty Canada faces with respect to industrial research and development is that American and other foreign-owned companies do no research in this country. As an expression of gross domestic product invested in research and development compared with other countries, we do extraordinarily poorly.
One of the strong suits of this Government should be its understanding of the economy and commitment to competitiveness. One of the obvious characteristics of the modem economic world is that a country like Canada cannot continue to be dependent exclusively on its forests, fisheries and mines in order to continue to thrive economically.
There are a number of reasons for this, having to do with the necessity of sustainable development and increased competition from alternative sources and the resources which have meant so much to Canada. Part of it is due to the substitution of other substances and materials in manufacture for the materials that we have dug from the ground and cut from our forests. It is clear that if Canada is to thrive in the future, it cannot function exclusively on the basis of the exploitation of our resources. It must function by harnessing the intelligence and the creativity of its people. That is fundamental.

This is not a new discovery on my part, but it is certainly true that this is a discovery that has had little impact in this place.
