Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and a pleasure for me to speak to this House today in support of the Speech from the Throne which outlines our goals for the future of Canada. The Throne Speech set out five main objectives through which this Government plans to build a strong and a united country. Our plan calls for the building of a stronger economy, for the protection of our environment, for a caring and compassionate society, for the fostering of values that make Canada unique, and for a commitment to national unity. I believe the implementation of these objectives and the challenge we face together will not only strengthen our Government but the people of Canada as a whole.
April 10, 1989

Today I would like to have had the time to comment on all of these objectives. However, with time constraints, I will be limiting my comments to the one issue that I feel must be of prime importance if we are to be successful with the remaining four objectives.
I refer to the national debt. The people of Alberta and the people of Canada are growing more and more concerned about the increasing national debt. Since 1984, this Conservative Government has made a concerted effort to control that debt and has lowered the deficit in a slow but steady way. However, now it is time for stronger measures, and virtually everyone, politicians of all stripes, 89 per cent of Canadians, business leaders, even social groups, agree that something should be done to reduce the $29 billion a year deficit and the build up of the federal debt which now totals approximately $320 billion.
The Throne Speech offers Canadians from sea to sea a vision of the future, a vision of Canada that is confident, unified and strong. It is a vision of Canada that holds a unique identity among nations, a Canada that leads the world community with new ideas. It is a vision of Canada that is vibrant and progressive but also caring and compassionate.
As a country and as individuals, we as Canadians have achieved much over the years, but now it is time to build for the future, to attain this vision, and to eradicate our national debt.
Why is the deficit a problem? It is often said that a deficit can be used to stimulate a weak economy and essentially this is true if it is used only over a short time. However, when it is used indiscriminately and over a long term it becomes a millstone that makes it virtually impossible for a Government to function effectively. That is where we are headed.
The number one threat to Canada's future is our national debt. Large government deficits mean higher interest rates. It means less investment and fewer jobs. Each year that there is a deficit, the debt grows. That means more and more money must be spent to pay interest on the debt.
Today, 31 cents out of every dollar spent by the federal Government goes to paying interest on our debt. In the long run this affects the ability of this Government, or any other Government, to provide the programs and the services that we as Canadians have come to appreciate.
The Address-Mrs. Feltham
Some Hon. Members have expressed a fear for the future of our social programs. I also have a fear that our social programs will suffer if we do not work to lower the deficit. For instance, at the present time the Government spends more money on interest payments than on old age security, guaranteed income supplements, spouses' allowance, housing, health, education, and family allowances, all combined.
I am sure we are all in agreement that the time for action is now. We must secure our social programs for the future. Democracy itself may be the reason for the rise in government spending, a government response to the ever-increasing demand for public goods and public services.
Increased government spending is a reflection of our response to events in society, to our social obligations, and to our political pledges to each other. From money paid to parents of a new child to cheques paid each month to senior citizens, the spending activities of government touch every part of our lives from the time we are bom until death. We eat bread produced with taxpayers' dollars. We wear clothing made by companies aided by grants. We live in homes financed by publicly backed mortgage funds.
Government spending helps us when we are sick. It provides the opportunity for education and it supports us when we are jobless. In Canada, government balance sheets are not simply facts and figures, a listing of contributions and distributions, they are a result of our collective wants. There is increasing pressure on political leaders to provide their citizens with these wants. The political reality is, however, that deficit reduction does not make good politics. However, I and a majority of Canadians know that something has to be done, and done now.
The public has now become aware of the implications of continuous overspending. It has elected this Government to ensure that the brakes are applied. This does not mean that our job will be an easy one. We must be decisive in our approach to debt reduction and we must educate our citizens on why it is necessary.
We know that not everyone will agree with the policies that are laid down, but it will be our job to ensure the transition between what was thought to be an endless amount of money and control of the national debt be thoughtfully proceeded with. This Government is fully aware that not everyone will agree with the policies that are laid down. I believe in this Government and its ability to rectify the situation. I believe that it has the capability to turn these dark times into good, sound economic times and restore a balance to government financing.

April 10, 1989
The Address-Mrs. Feltham
In Alberta there are 26 constituencies and today we have 24 Conservative Members in the House of Commons. Many people would have us believe that the Conservative rode to victory on the back of free trade. That may have been one of the reasons, but the reduction of the national debt most assuredly carried as much importance, especially in my riding, as did the free trade debate. I know from listening to the people of my riding that the grass roots re-elected this Government because they know that the national debt is the number one problem in this country and that this Government would, at the beginning of its mandate, take strong measures to attack that national debt.
How do we reconcile these two objectives: the national debt and a caring and a compassionate Government? Is it possible to bridge that gap? We have spoken about bridging a gap when we refer to a relationship between a parent and a child or between a reporter and a newspaper, but now we are looking at it between deficits and social programs.
Will those two become reconcilable, and where? On April 27, when my hon. colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), brings in the Budget, I know that all considerations will have been given to these complex issues. We will still be considered a Government which is compassionate and caring, but a Government which is strong enough to face the realities of its responsibility. Canadians have told this Government that it is time to bring the national debt under control. This is the year, not next year, not two years from now, but on April 27, 1989.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for Wild Rose (Mrs. Feltham) on her speech and her description of the importance of deficit reduction. Indeed I come from a riding in Alberta, and there it was the number one issue throughout the entire election campaign. My colleague also spoke about the Free Trade Agreement, but deficit reduction was number one out where I come from.
It is interesting to note that in 1967 when the Right Hon. Pierre Trudeau came into power, the debt was sitting at $18 billion and when he left it was at $220 billion. In fact, it was growing at approximately 24 per cent per year.
We did tackle the debt in 1984. We were able to cut our spending and bring the deficit down from about $38.7 billion to $28.9 billion. We talked about rising interest rates. Rising interest rates will not control inflation. We simply have to lower the deficit and the debt.
What my colleague said was pretty interesting. She said that 31 cents on every dollar the federal Government takes in, in revenues, goes to service this debt, and she was quite right. If we do not tackle it now, that will go up and up.
I want the Hon. Member to comment on one area. She spoke about a strong and united Canada and a national unity. Just prior to her speaking, I heard members of the Liberal Party talking about forward thinking programs and how they would unite Canada.
I wonder if my colleague might refresh the memories of our Liberal colleagues about what happened in 1981 with a program called the National Energy Program which zeroed in on one industry in particular and what happened to Western Canada under those forward thinking policies. Those policies devastated us. I would ask the the Hon. Member for Wild Rose what she has to say about what happened to Alberta and indeed to western Canada under that forward thinking program.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for her question. When she said it was devastating, she summed it up and I do not think I can add anything further to that. The effect it had on Alberta was devastating.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we all worry about the deficit and about putting government spending under control. Not one single Hon. Member here disagrees with some sort of control. The question is how to do this. Do we cut baby bonuses? Do we cut unemployment insurance? What programs do we tackle in order to reduce the deficit?
We in the Liberal Party introduced a package during the election campaign. We spoke about reducing the deficit through job creation, through infrastructure programs, through retraining programs, through investment in research and development, through investment in education, through combating illiteracy. Because of illiteracy by itself, company after company in the private sector has indicated that they are losing in the vicinity $10 billion annually.
April 10, 1989

The Government should be looking at those things. It is dandy to be talking about cutting the deficit, but there are other means available to the Government in terms of investment in the future of our children, investment in research and development, investment in education and investment in employment retraining, particularly for those who are in their forties and early fifties. We are interested in seeing the Government do something about those kinds of investments, and we will be watching fairly closely to see what will be done.
Dealing with the environment, if the past four years is any indication of what this Government will do, we are in for a rough ride. Of course Canadians voted for the Conservatives, but did they give a majority to the Conservatives in terms of popular vote? No, over 50 per cent of the people of Canada did not vote for Conservative programs and did not go along with the Conservative's ideas.
One must reflect on what we are doing for the future of Canada and what we are investing in the future of our children. We must talk about economic development. Trade by itself is a flashy issue. However, when talking about trade, a very important issue is putting infrastructure in place.
Look at what will happen to the infrastructure of Canada over the next 10 years. In the United States, infrastructure is the number one issue. The United States Government is trying to address that issue. What are we doing here in Canada in terms of investment in infrastructure or sewage treatment plants which, since 1984, have had not one penny put into them? Through one single area, investment in infrastructure, we can generate hundreds of thousands of jobs.
I know that there are many people in this room with municipal backgrounds. I will be watching closely to see what they will do. When they were in municipal politics, they all spoke about government investment in infrastructure. Now we will see delivery. Now we will see commitment.
It is great to talk about deficit reduction, but it is equally important to talk about productivity, education and training for older employees.
The Address-Mrs. Feltham
I did not want to ask a question because I already know the answer. We have been given a whitewash for the past four years and I hope we will not be given the same whitewash over the next four years. I will wait patiently to see what kind of programs there will be for the environment, infrastructure, education and combating illiteracy. Those are the four important issues I would like to see the Government do something about.
The future does not look too bright. We can tighten the belt, but it is important to make sure that we do not cut our throats at the same time.
Canada is a leading nation in the industrialized world. We have to maintain that role. We must carry on, and we can only carry on by investing in the future of Canadians. We can only carry on by investing in education.
Look at how much we are investing in education. Look at the number of people in Canada who are functionally illiterate. One in every five is considered illiterate.
